explanation: The pattern follows the decision's pace. Files and replicas refreshed daily or weekly suit slow decisions; APIs and queues serve decisions taken within the hour.

stem: Your agent will start writing confirmed schedules back to the MES. What must the write path include?
a: Validation before each write and an audit trail of every change
b: Direct inserts into the MES tables, which are faster than going through any API
c: A nightly batch that overwrites the whole MES schedule
d: Automatic retries until the MES accepts each record
explanation: Read first; write back with validation and an audit trail. Retrying until accepted or overwriting in bulk hides errors in a system of record.

stem: A pilot needs ERP data in week one, but API access requires a security review. What is a sensible start?
a: Screen-scrape the ERP using a shared user account
b: Pause all work until the API review is complete
c: Ask IT for direct write access to the ERP database while the review runs
d: A scheduled read-only extract while the API review proceeds
explanation: File extracts are a legitimate first integration pattern. They let work start safely while the next rung, API access, is reviewed.

stem: Machine stop events can come from a message queue or from polling the database every minute. What does the queue add?
a: It removes the need to validate the incoming data
b: Events arrive as they happen, without loading the source
c: It stores the full event history, so the plant historian can be retired
d: It lets the agent write back without human approval
explanation: A queue pushes events to consumers when they occur. Polling adds load on the source and delay, and neither pattern removes validation.

stem: In the three-layer data census, which three layers do you inventory?
a: Raw, cleaned and aggregated data
b: Master data, transactional data and reference data
c: System data, spreadsheet data and data in heads
d: Plant, regional and group-level data
explanation: The census asks where each needed fact lives: in systems, in spreadsheets or only in people's heads. The last two layers are often the largest.

stem: Your census finds the real changeover rules only in a senior planner's memory. What is the right next step?
a: Walk real cases with the planner and record the rules in a structured form
b: Leave them out of scope until someone documents them in the ERP
c: Use the ERP's standard changeover times as a proxy
d: Let the model infer them from historical schedules without the planner's input
explanation: Data in heads is extracted by sitting with the expert on real cases. ERP standards miss the rules, and history alone cannot tell rules from habits.

stem: Why run the data census before committing to a delivery date?
a: It replaces the need for interviews with operators and planners
b: It tells IT which systems need upgrading before the project starts
c: It proves to finance that the baseline is reliable
d: The share of data outside systems drives the extraction effort
explanation: Data in spreadsheets and heads must be extracted by hand, which takes time. The census sizes that work before a date is promised.

stem: A quality engineer's spreadsheet holds the only list of approved material substitutions. How should the pipeline treat it?
a: Copy it once at the start of the project and stop updating it
b: As a source with a named owner, a fixed format and checks on load
c: Ignore it, because only data held in systems can be trusted in production
d: Ask the engineer to email changes to the team when they remember
explanation: Spreadsheet data is real data. Give it an owner, a format and load checks so it can feed production like any other source.

stem: The MES logs 2% downtime on a press, yet output is 20% below a rate verified on the floor. What should you suspect first?
a: Operators overstating the parts they produce
b: A rounding error in how the MES stores durations
c: Unlogged micro-stops and slow cycles
d: Scrap being counted twice in the output total
explanation: Short stops and slow cycles rarely reach the downtime log. Data archaeology compares logged events with what the floor actually shows.

stem: Logs show 90-minute changeovers; the procedure takes 40. Interviews reveal routine maintenance during changeovers. What follows?
a: Maintenance is hidden in changeover time and must be separated
b: The procedure is wrong and should be rewritten as 90 minutes
c: Operators are slow at changeovers and need retraining
d: The logs are unreliable and should be dropped from the analysis
explanation: Maintenance hidden inside changeovers is classic data archaeology. Separating the two shows the true changeover time and the real maintenance load.

stem: A press's stop log tags 60% of stops as 'other'. What is the best use of this data?
a: Model those stops as random noise in the capacity plan
b: Delete the 'other' stops so that the reason analysis stays clean
c: Rely only on the 40% of stops that have a reason
d: Treat it as a lead and observe stops on the floor
explanation: Poor logs point to where the real causes hide. Going to the floor recovers them; discarding or modeling them as noise loses the signal.

stem: Why compare logged downtime with downtime observed on the floor before modeling capacity?
a: Observed downtime is usually exaggerated by operators
b: Logged downtime is often understated, which overstates capacity
c: The comparison is needed to calibrate the machine sensors on the line
d: Auditors require it before any model goes live
explanation: Logs miss micro-stops and mislabel events. A model fed logged downtime assumes capacity the plant does not have.

stem: An orders table that usually loads 2 million rows loads 200,000 tonight. Which check stops this reaching users?
a: A schema check that the column names and types are unchanged
b: A longer timeout on the load job
c: A row-count check against expected volume
d: A file compression ratio alert
explanation: Checks at each stage, such as row counts, null rates and ranges, catch partial loads. A schema check passes because the columns are fine.

stem: Your pipeline reloads the full order history every hour and keeps getting slower. What is the standard fix?
a: Incremental loads of changed rows, keyed on stable business keys
b: More frequent full reloads, so that each run has less new data to absorb
c: Dropping all history older than one month from the pipeline
d: Moving the same full reload to a larger server
explanation: Incremental loads with upserts on business keys process only what changed. Full reloads grow with history however often they run.

stem: The ERP team renames a column and your agent silently receives nulls for a week. What would have prevented this?
a: Running the pipeline twice as often
b: Granting the agent write access to the ERP
c: Keeping every raw extract for a longer retention period before deletion
d: A data contract with the source team, plus null-rate checks
explanation: A data contract fixes what the source delivers and who announces changes. Null-rate checks catch breaks the contract missed, on the first run.

stem: A temperature feed suddenly shows 1,500 °C for a process that runs at 200 °C. Which check should catch it?
a: A duplicate check on the record keys
b: A row-count check on the batch
c: A range check at ingestion that holds or flags the data
d: A freshness check that the latest timestamp is recent enough
explanation: Range checks catch values outside physical limits. Row counts and freshness would pass, because the data arrived complete and on time.

stem: You join orders to order lines, then sum order value. The total is three times too high. Why?
a: The inner join silently dropped every order that had no order lines at all
b: Each order repeats once per line, so its value is counted per line
c: Order values are stored in the wrong currency
d: The sum function rounds every value upward
explanation: A join to a many side repeats the one side's columns. Sum order-level values before joining, or sum at line level.

stem: You need every machine with its count of stops this week, including machines with no stops. Which join?
a: A left join from machines to stops
b: An inner join between machines and stops
c: An inner join from stops to machines
d: A cross join between machines and stops
explanation: A left join keeps every machine and counts zero where no stop matches. An inner join silently drops the machines with no stops.

stem: An inner join between orders and the customer table drops 5% of orders. What is the most likely cause?
a: The customer table is too large for the join to finish
b: The orders are duplicated in the source system and removed by the join
c: The join should use a window function instead
d: Those orders carry customer IDs missing from the customer table
explanation: An inner join keeps only matching rows. Orphan keys, often from data entry or migration, vanish silently; a left join and a null check reveal them.

stem: You need each machine's running seven-day average scrap rate. Which SQL feature fits best?
a: A GROUP BY on machine only
b: A DISTINCT on machine and day
c: A window function partitioned by machine, ordered by day
d: A self-join of every row to every other row in the table
explanation: Window functions compute running values per partition without collapsing rows. A GROUP BY on machine gives one figure for the whole period.

stem: Average cycle time per product is computed as the average of daily averages. What is the problem?
a: Days with few parts weigh as much as busy days
b: Daily averages cannot be stored as decimal numbers
c: The result double counts parts made across midnight
d: The daily averages should have been summed instead
explanation: An unweighted average of averages ignores volume. Sum cycle time and parts over the whole period, then divide.

stem: Two plants in different time zones send events in local time. What should the pipeline do?
a: Convert everything to the headquarters' local time
b: Keep each plant's local times and compare the plants hour by hour
c: Drop the time part and keep only the date of each event
d: Store timestamps in UTC and keep each source's time zone
explanation: UTC makes events comparable and safe across daylight saving changes; keeping the source zone lets you rebuild local shift views.

stem: A capacity model gives every machine 24 hours a day, but the plant runs two shifts and stops on weekends. What is missing?
a: The machines' standard rates from the ERP
b: The shift calendar, which defines available hours
c: The OEE target set for each machine
d: The historian's raw signal feed
explanation: Available time comes from the shift calendar, holidays and planned stops. Without it, capacity is overstated by a large factor.

stem: One system records resin in kilograms, another in 25 kg bags. What should the pipeline do?
a: Let each downstream user convert the units when needed
b: Convert to one unit explicitly, with the factor stored and tested
c: Keep the larger figure when the two systems disagree
d: Treat both figures as the same unit to keep things simple
explanation: Units of measure must be explicit. A stored, tested conversion factor avoids silent errors of 25 times in stock and consumption.

stem: A complaint names a defective finished lot. What data shows which raw material lots went into it?
a: Lot genealogy linking consumed lots to produced lots
b: The bill of materials for the finished product
c: The supplier's certificate of analysis for each delivery
d: The production order's planned start and end dates
explanation: The bill of materials says what should be used; genealogy records which actual lots were consumed. Only genealogy supports a trace or a recall.

stem: A night shift runs from 10 pm to 6 am, and output is grouped by calendar day. What goes wrong?
a: Output is counted twice in the weekly totals
b: The night shift's data cannot be stored by the MES
c: Day shifts appear less productive than they are
d: Each night shift's output splits across two days
explanation: Shift-based metrics need the shift calendar, not midnight boundaries. Splitting a shift across two days distorts per-shift and per-day figures.

stem: Your agent sets confirmed due dates. The ERP owns that field and the APS holds a copy. Where should the agent write?
a: To the ERP, which then feeds the copy in the APS
b: To both systems at once, so that they stay aligned
c: To whichever system the planner happens to have open
d: To a new table the agent owns, read by both systems
explanation: Writes go to the owner system; copies refresh from it. Writing to two places creates two owners and, soon, two truths.

stem: Users edit item weights in the WMS copy, which now disagrees with the ERP that owns them. What is the fix?
a: Sync the WMS edits back to overwrite the ERP every night
b: Let each system keep its own value for its own purposes
c: Make edits in the ERP and refresh the WMS copy from it
d: Average the two weights in a nightly reconciliation job
explanation: Every field has one owner; other sources are copies that never take edits. Syncing edits back makes the copy a second owner.

stem: Your agent reads orders and writes schedule proposals. How should its service account be set up?
a: With administrator rights, to avoid access errors in production
b: With only the permissions those two tasks need
c: Under a named planner's login, so actions are traceable
d: As one shared account for all of the project's tools
explanation: Least privilege limits damage when something goes wrong. A dedicated, logged service account is traceable without borrowing a person's login.

stem: A database password appears in the pipeline's code repository. What should be done?
a: Make the repository private so that outsiders cannot see it
b: Rename the variable so the password is harder to spot
c: Leave it, since only the project team can read the code
d: Rotate it and move secrets to a store outside the code
explanation: Secrets live outside code. Once exposed, a password is compromised, so it is rotated; hiding the repository leaves it in the history.

stem: An agent's write-back changed 40 orders overnight and planners ask why. What should already exist?
a: A rollback script that reverts all changes made by the agent
b: A rule that the agent writes only during the day shift
c: An audit log of each action, its inputs and the account used
d: A weekly summary email sent to the planners by the team
explanation: Audit logs make every automated write explainable: what changed, on which inputs, under which account. Without them nobody can answer the planners.

stem: A teammate asks a coding assistant to compute plant OEE from a shift log nobody has opened yet. What should happen first?
a: Profile the file: counts per date and shift, ranges, duplicates, gaps, units
b: Ask the model for a typical industry OEE figure to use as a sanity check on the result
c: Let the tool clean every anomaly it finds automatically, then compute
d: Compute OEE first, then look for outliers if the figure seems odd
explanation: Profiling before computing is the first verification habit: anomalies change the result and must be decided by the team. Cleaning automatically hides the decisions; checking against an industry figure checks nothing about this file.

stem: Profiling a shift log, you find one line reporting about 12,000 t in shifts where its peers make about 14 t. What is the right move?
a: Delete those rows as outliers and carry on with the analysis
b: Keep them, since extreme values average out over ninety days
c: Flag a probable kilogram entry in the data notes and confirm with the site
d: Divide them by 1,000 in the code, since the unit error is obvious to anyone
explanation: Quarantine with a reason; never fix silently. The likely unit error is recorded, the handling is decided with the team and confirmed with the site. Dividing silently may be right, but nobody can check or trust a correction that was never written down.

stem: Seven rows in a shift log repeat the same date, shift and machine with identical values in every column. How do you handle them?
a: Keep them, since each one may record a second run of the line
b: Remove the exact copies and record how many, and why, in the data notes
c: Average each pair of rows into a single row before computing
d: Leave them, since seven rows barely move a quarterly figure for the plant
explanation: Identical rows on the key date, shift and machine are duplicates: they double count output and minutes. Remove them and write the decision down so another pair can check it. 'Too small to matter' is a silent assumption.

stem: Your app shows availability as the mean of each row's run/planned ratio, and three rows have zero planned minutes. What is the sound approach?
a: Average the row ratios, skipping rows where planned time is zero
b: Average per machine first, then average the seven machine figures
c: Replace zero planned time with 480 minutes so every row has a ratio
d: Sum run minutes and planned minutes over the period, then divide
explanation: Ratios are computed from sums: a short or idle shift must not weigh like a full one. Summing first also handles zero planned time without inventing minutes, as setting 480 would.

stem: Pair B computes M07 OEE at 61% by hand; the app shows 66%. The demo is in ten minutes. What does the course expect?
a: Show the app's figure, since it is computed in code from the CSV
b: Show the average of the two values and mention the uncertainty
c: Find which assumption differs, or explain the gap, before showing it
d: Show Pair B's figure, since a manual check is the more reliable one
explanation: Every number shown must survive someone else's check: demo only when both pairs agree or can explain the difference. Code is not right because it is code; a hand calculation is not right because it is manual.

stem: Your daily output uses the shift-start date, so the 22:00 to 06:00 shift counts on the day it began. Finance reports from midnight. What do you do?
a: Nothing, since both conventions give the same daily totals over a full month
b: Split each night shift's output evenly across the two days
c: Move every night shift to the next day to match finance
d: State the convention and agree with finance on one before comparing
explanation: Shift calendars are a silent assumption: the two conventions give different daily figures. Write the convention down and agree it with the people who will compare numbers, rather than reshaping the data on a guess.

stem: One line's minutes per changeover are double the other lines'. A shift leader says the crew cleans the screen pack during changeovers. What follows?
a: Maintenance is hidden in changeover time; separate it before modeling changeovers
b: That line's products are harder to change; give it a longer changeover rule in the model
c: The log is wrong for that line; exclude it from the changeover analysis
d: Changeovers are the problem on that line; target them for reduction first
explanation: Data archaeology: logged categories mix activities. Cleaning done during changeovers inflates changeover time and hides maintenance, so a rule or target built on the raw figure is wrong.

stem: A line logs little downtime, yet its output is well below run minutes times the nameplate rate. What should you check first?
a: Lower the nameplate rate until the performance figure looks normal
b: Short stops and slow running that nobody logs, observed on the floor
c: Whether scrap is counted twice in the line's quality figure
d: Whether the planned minutes wrongly include the line's weekend shutdowns
explanation: A gap between logged run time and output usually means unlogged micro-stops or slow cycles. Watch the line before trusting the log; tuning the rate to fit the result hides the loss.

stem: The procedure says the weekly plan is frozen; the planner says she rewrites it daily. How do you establish how often it really changes?
a: Ask the planner to estimate how many changes she makes in a week
b: Survey the shift leaders on how stable they find the published weekly plan
c: Count change events and saved plan versions with code, by type and horizon
d: Reread the procedure and the ERP flow for the exceptions they allow
explanation: The procedure is a hypothesis and the change log is the evidence. Loops are computed from data with code you can show, not estimated in interviews or read from the stated process.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture

stem: Interviews say the plan changes all the time, yet the ERP shows few changes. Most changes are keyed into it days later, or never. What follows?
a: The interviews exaggerate, since the ERP is the system of record
b: The ERP is unreliable and should be replaced before any planning work starts
c: Late keying does not matter, since the changes do reach the ERP
d: The ERP reflects the official process and understates the real loop
explanation: Data produced by the official process can mislead: the ERP holds what was keyed, when it was keyed. The real loop is measured from the sources where changes happen. The ERP stays the system of record for orders.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture

stem: You ask an AI assistant to infer the real planning steps from eight interviews. What makes its output usable on the as-is map?
a: Each step cites a file and line, and you check a sample against the sources
b: A confident summary without citations, which keeps the as-is map short and easy to read
c: Its synthesis as it is, since it has read every interview in full
d: Only the steps that match the written procedure, to avoid noise
explanation: Use the model as an analyst you check, not an oracle: every step of the true process cites a file, and someone verifies samples. Keeping only steps that match the procedure throws away the true process.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture

stem: The ERP holds orders and one changeover time for all products; the planner's whiteboard holds real times by family. Who owns each fact?
a: The ERP owns both, since it is the system of record
b: The ERP owns the order; the planner owns the changeover rule
c: The planner owns both, since her figures are more accurate
d: Ownership is shared, with a weekly reconciliation of the two
explanation: One owner per fact: the ontology says which system or person owns it. The ERP is right about orders and wrong about changeovers; the planner's rule gets an id, a source and her as owner.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture

stem: You consolidate plan changes from a clerk's notebook, a mailbox, line comments and lab records into one log. What makes it fit to use?
a: A model reviews the merged file and removes inconsistent rows
b: The ERP confirms each event, since it is the system of record
c: The clerk who logs the changes checks it against her own record
d: Nothing more, since each source is first-hand and can be trusted as it is
explanation: A merged log is only evidence once the person who knows the changes has checked it. The ERP cannot confirm events that were never keyed into it, and a model removing rows is a silent fix.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture

stem: Line logs arrive as one CSV a day at 06:00, but your repair loop must react to a breakdown within minutes. What do you do?
a: Capture breakdowns as they happen in an intake app, and ask for faster exports
b: Run the repair loop on the 06:00 file and accept a day of delay on every event
c: Have a model predict today's breakdowns from last year's logs
d: Poll the shared folder every minute in case a newer file appears
explanation: A daily batch means deciding on yesterday's plant. Capture the event at the source when it happens, and ask the vendor or IT for a faster feed; polling a folder does not make the file arrive sooner.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop

stem: Lab results are stored by batch number and orders by order number, with nothing linking them. A quality hold must reach the right order. What is the durable fix?
a: Match batches to orders by date proximity in a nightly script
b: Ask the model to guess the order from the lab comment text
c: Build a new database that holds both and replaces the lab system
d: Have the lab record the order number at entry, with an owner
explanation: When the link does not exist, capture it at the source with an owner for the field. Matching by date or model guesses breaks silently, and a new database nobody owns becomes an orphan.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop

stem: Customer change requests arrive in a key account manager's private mailbox. Your event reader needs them. What is the right access route?
a: Store his mailbox credentials in the connector's configuration file
b: A shared planning mailbox, created by IT, that the connector reads
c: A forwarding rule set up quietly from his personal mailbox
d: Ask him to key every request into the ERP first, then read the ERP
explanation: Access is granted, not taken: IT creates a shared mailbox the connector may read, and the private mailbox stays private. Borrowed credentials and quiet forwarding break least privilege and trust.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop

stem: A scheduling clerk's paper notebook is the only record of plan changes since February. How should the team treat it?
a: Ignore it, since paper records are not reliable enough
b: Photograph it and let a model infer the rules from it
c: Type it with her consent, check it with her, then capture changes in an app
d: Wait for a new MES that will log every plan change automatically, with timestamps
explanation: Much of the data agents need lives outside systems. Bring it in with its owner's consent and check, then build a mini-app so new changes are captured structured and timed.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop

stem: Your connectors show which orders the planner moved in the plan, but not why. Where should the reason come from?
a: An override screen that asks her for a reason each time
b: The ERP change history, which records each edit and its author
c: A model that infers likely reasons from the order data
d: A monthly interview in which she reviews all her changes
explanation: The reason lives only in the planner's head, so a mini-app collects it at the moment of the override. Each reason then becomes a rule, a data fix or a decision; the ERP records the edit, not the why.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop

stem: Your platform includes an ERP write-back connector for published plans. On the first day of the pilot, what state should it be in?
a: Enabled, with the agent writing only orders it is confident about
b: Enabled for the planner's account and disabled for every agent
c: Removed from the build until the whole pilot has finished
d: Built but disabled, until the IT owner enables it after tests
explanation: Read first; write back with validation and an audit trail, each step earned. The write-back exists, stays off by default and is enabled by IT once tests and a runbook exist. Confidence is not permission.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop

stem: You take a planning system to a second plant whose shop-floor data sits in a different MES. What do you rebuild there?
a: The ontology core, since each plant names things differently
b: The data connectors and field mapping, plus the local rules
c: The solver, tuned to the new plant's data format
d: Nothing, since the group ERP is the same on every site
explanation: Reuse the core, rebuild the edge: the ontology, platform and solvers are reused; connectors, field mappings and local rules are rebuilt per site. A shared ERP does not mean shared shop-floor data.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: One plant in a rollout records production on paper. A model will need its stop and output data. What is the plan?
a: Skip the plant until it has bought and installed an MES
b: Use the group ERP figures, which already cover every site
c: Capture at the source with a simple form for weeks before relying on it
d: Estimate its data from a similar plant in the group that already runs an MES
explanation: When the data does not exist, create it at the source: a form or a sensor, for a few weeks, before any model depends on it. Borrowed or estimated data describes another plant.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: The line logger's vendor says its product has no API, and you need its data next week. What is the first move?
a: Use the file it already writes, or a database view agreed with IT
b: Scrape its screens with a script that nobody at the client maintains
c: Wait until the vendor's roadmap adds an API to the product
d: Ask operators to re-key the data into a shared spreadsheet
explanation: Dead ends have known moves: ask the vendor, use the export it already produces, or read a view with IT. Screen scraping creates an orphan; re-keying adds a source of error and work for operators.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: The ERP and the planner's spreadsheet give different line speeds. Planning uses one and finance the other. What is the move?
a: Use the average of the two values in the solver
b: Let the model choose the more plausible of the two values on each solver run
c: Use the higher speed, which matches the plant's targets
d: Name the source of truth with its owner; reconcile with finance
explanation: When two systems disagree, decide which one counts with the owner, object by object, and reconcile regularly with finance. Averaging or letting a model choose gives a number nobody owns.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: Your Verifier finds the scrap baseline double counts a component, so the gain shown to the controller is a third too high. What do you do?
a: Correct it quietly in next month's report
b: Tell sponsor and controller within a day, with the corrected figure
c: Wait to present it at Friday's steering committee
d: Keep the figure for now and offset it with a new gain found in the coming weeks
explanation: Announce a data error first, with the corrected number and the check that would have caught it. Trust lost by a correction comes back; trust lost by a cover-up does not.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: A model needs the reason for each stop, but the logger's comment field is free text and mostly empty. What do you do?
a: Add a reason code at the source and collect it for a few weeks first
b: Let the model infer stop reasons from the comments that do exist
c: Build the model without reasons and add them after go-live
d: Ask maintenance to rebuild last year's reasons from memory
explanation: Data that does not exist is captured at the source, structured, for a period long enough to use. Inferring from sparse text or memory gives guesses that look like data.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: Group security needs six weeks to review any new cloud service, and your plan assumed live data access in week one. What do you do?
a: Run the pilot on a personal cloud account until the review ends
b: Ask the sponsor to waive the security review for a short, low-risk pilot
c: Start the review on day one and work on agreed exports meanwhile
d: Pause the project until the review has been completed
explanation: Start the security review on day one and work on read-only exports while it runs. Shortcutting the rules, or waiting idle, both cost more than the six weeks.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: Group IT requires plant data to stay in the EU, on the group's own tenant. How do you set up the multi-site platform?
a: Copy each site's data to your own cloud for faster development
b: Deploy the software in the client's tenant, under its access rules
c: Anonymize the data and move it to a central vendor data lake
d: Ask for an exception at the pilot site, then comply with the rule at the other sites
explanation: Bring the software to the data: it runs on the client's servers, in their tenant and region, with secrets in a vault and access per role, the same on every site.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: Your loader appends each day's event file. A corrected file is resent and every event in it now appears twice. What is the fix?
a: Truncate the table and reload the full history every night
b: Ask the source system never to resend a corrected file
c: Upsert on a stable business key, so reloading a file is harmless
d: Remove the duplicates in each dashboard query, at display time, for every chart
explanation: An idempotent pipeline gives the same result however often it runs: stable business keys and upserts make reloads and corrections safe. Full reloads grow slower; fixing at display leaves the data wrong.

stem: After a vendor update, one of two daily exports arrives with its columns in a new order. What should the pipeline do?
a: Map the columns by position and load the file as usual
b: Stop the whole pipeline until the vendor has answered
c: Load it anyway and let the model detect and correct the mismatched fields afterwards
d: Quarantine that file with a reason, load the other, alert the owner
explanation: Quarantine with a reason; never fix silently. The suspect file is held and named, the good one flows, and the owner fixes the cause. Loading by position silently writes values into the wrong fields.

stem: You join orders to change events to count late orders per customer. The count exceeds the number of orders. Why?
a: The join drops orders that have no change events at all
b: Orders with several events appear once per event; count distinct orders
c: Late orders are counted twice because of time zone offsets
d: The change log holds events for orders not in the order table
explanation: A one-to-many join repeats each order per matching event, so counts and sums inflate. Count distinct order keys, or aggregate events before joining.

stem: You join lines to breakdowns and count per line for this month. Lines with no breakdowns are missing from the report. What happened?
a: An inner join dropped lines with no match; use a left join from lines
b: The breakdown table is incomplete and needs reloading from source
c: COUNT drops any line whose breakdown total is zero, by design
d: The lines table has duplicate keys that cancel each other out
explanation: An inner join keeps only rows that match on both sides. A left join from the lines table keeps every line, with a zero count where there were no breakdowns.

stem: An agent reads incoming emails and turns them into planning events. Which grants should its service identity have?
a: Propose and confirm events, so the planner is spared routine clicks
b: Read the ERP fully, so it can check every order it finds in emails
c: Propose events only: no confirming, publishing or ERP writes
d: The same rights as the planner, so the two can work interchangeably
explanation: Least privilege: the event reader may propose; a person confirms and the planner publishes. Narrow grants are what stop a hidden instruction in an email from changing the plan.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop

stem: Planners ask why twelve orders moved overnight. What should let you answer within minutes?
a: The model's chat history for the night, if it was kept
b: A rerun of last night's solver with the same parameters
c: A comparison of the ERP order table before and after
d: An audit line per decision and write, with actor and rule ids
explanation: Observability is a platform layer: every decision, tool call and write leaves an audit line naming the actor and the rules behind it. A before and after comparison shows what moved, not why.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop

stem: A team wants a planning tool to read machine stops directly from the line controllers. What is usually the better source?
a: Stop events from the MES or historian, above the control level
b: The ERP, which records every stop as it happens on the line
c: A model that estimates stops from hourly output figures
d: The controllers themselves, polled every second by the planning tool
explanation: In ISA-95 terms, levels 0 to 2 are sensing and control; the MES and historians at level 3 turn signals into stop events. A planning tool reads those, without touching the control layer.

stem: Your kickoff document for the executive committee must name the data source of the gains baseline. Which source should it be?
a: Your own pipeline, since it is cleaner than the client's systems
b: The system finance already trusts, with the controller as its owner
c: The vendor's benchmark figures for comparable plants in the sector
d: The dashboard the team built during pre-sales
explanation: The baseline comes from the system finance already trusts and is owned by the controller, fixed in week one. A gain measured from your own pipeline is one the controller cannot compute without you.

stem: Your census shows that about 40% of the facts the planning tool needs exist in no system. What follows for the plan?
a: Delay the start until IT has loaded those facts into the ERP
b: Build on system data now and add the rest after go-live
c: Let the model infer the missing facts from historical data
d: Budget time with the experts and mini-apps to capture them
explanation: About 40% of the data agents need lives in heads and spreadsheets, as the course's field figure says. Extracting it on site is planned work, not a gap to defer or guess.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture

stem: A proposed AI use case cannot be sized in euros before work starts. What does the course recommend?
a: Do not start it: unsized gains are rarely captured
b: Run a pilot first, since the value will become clear
c: Size it after go-live, using real usage data
d: Use the vendor's ROI benchmark for similar sites
explanation: Approve AI work like capex: a euro figure, an owner and a stop date before any code. A gain that cannot be sized up front is rarely captured later.

stem: Scheduling software frees 3,000 hours a year. When do those hours become money?
a: As soon as the software goes live on the site
b: When the software licence has been fully paid off by the savings
c: When someone decides to fill them with orders or cut overtime
d: At the next annual budget review
explanation: Software frees capacity; only decisions turn it into money. Capture needs an owner with the mandate to take those decisions.

stem: Which gain counts as validated in the FDE School's sense?
a: Any gain the project team can model credibly
b: The output of the vendor's ROI calculator for the site
c: The projected gains of the next three sites in the planned rollout
d: A measurable, attributable gain signed off by client finance
explanation: A gain exists once the client's finance team signs it. Models, vendor calculators and pipeline do not count.

stem: Your teams submit 40 ideas for AI use cases. What does the course recommend doing with the list?
a: Fund a small pilot for each idea and keep the ones that seem to work
b: Rank the ideas by how quickly each one can be built
c: Keep the few that move margin, sized in euros; refuse most
d: Start with the ideas that have the most staff support
explanation: Start from the P&L: pick the few decisions that move margin and put a euro figure on each before any code. Piloting everything spreads effort over ideas that will never pay.

stem: Polymex Industries can fund one AI project this year. Which target best fits the course's P&L-first approach?
a: Deciding the order sequence on the line that limits output
b: Summarizing meeting notes for every plant manager
c: A chatbot answering staff questions on HR policy
d: Helping the sales team write routine customer emails faster
explanation: The course targets the few decisions that move margin: what to schedule, buy, release or quote. Sequencing the line that limits output is one; the others save minutes, not margin.

stem: Ferralux has €500M in revenue. A use case credibly promises one point of margin. How should its CEO read that?
a: About €50K a year: too small to matter
b: About €500K a year: fine for a local pilot
c: About €5M a year: worth changing how a plant works
d: About €50M a year: enough to fund a new plant
explanation: One point of margin on €500M is €5M a year, the scale the course considers worth changing how a plant works.

stem: A vendor promises a 10% efficiency improvement on your scheduling. What is the course's view of that target?
a: Solid: any measurable gain is worth having
b: Too low: aim for multiples, since 10% rarely pays for the change
c: Acceptable, provided the vendor is willing to guarantee it in the contract
d: Good, as long as it shows within the first quarter
explanation: A 10% improvement rarely pays for the change it demands on the floor. Aim for multiples; a contract guarantee does not fix a target that is too small.

stem: You report on the AI program to the board. Which figure should lead the report?
a: The number of AI use cases now live across sites
b: The share of staff who use AI tools every week
c: The hours saved, as reported by users in surveys
d: Euro gains signed off by the finance team
explanation: A gain exists only once the client's finance team signs it. Use cases live, usage and self-reported hours measure activity, not money.

stem: A tool has freed hours on the line for six months, yet overtime spending has not moved. What is most likely missing?
a: More time for the tool to show its full results
b: Further training for staff on the tool's dashboards
c: A decision, by someone with the mandate, to cut the overtime
d: A more accurate and detailed model of machine capacity inside the tool
explanation: Software frees capacity; only decisions turn it into money. Waiting longer changes nothing if nobody decides to stop the overtime.

stem: Your committee approves an AI project with a euro target and a named owner. Like any capex, what else must the approval set?
a: A date to stop it if the target is not in sight
b: A commitment to roll it out to every site afterwards
c: An open exploration budget for the first year
d: A shortlist of AI models to compare before starting
explanation: Approve AI projects like capex: a euro figure, an owner and a date to stop. Without a stop date, failing projects drift on.

stem: After a year, 3 of your 10 AI initiatives have been stopped for missing their targets. How should the board read this?
a: As a sign the program is being poorly managed
b: As a reason to pause all new AI initiatives for at least a year
c: As proof the technology is not mature enough yet
d: As expected: about 30% fail, and stopping early is sound
explanation: The course expects about 30% of initiatives to fail and asks for them to be stopped early. A portfolio with no failures is usually not stopping anything.

stem: At its review date, an AI initiative is clearly off its euro target, and the team asks for six more months. What does the course advise?
a: Stop it now and move the people to a better use case
b: Grant the extension, since AI projects need time to mature
c: Keep it running quietly without reporting the delay
d: Double the budget so it can reach the target faster
explanation: Some initiatives fail; the discipline is to stop them early. Extending a project that is clearly off target delays the inevitable and ties up scarce people.

stem: Your CFO's AI case rests almost entirely on cutting operator headcount. What does the course expect to find?
a: That headcount is rightly where most of the value sits
b: That labor is usually a minority; bigger gains sit elsewhere
c: That no AI case should ever include labor savings
d: That headcount cuts are the quickest and easiest gains for finance to validate
explanation: Direct labor productivity is usually at most about a quarter of the value. Larger gains sit in working capital, speed to revenue, quality and deferred capex.

stem: A tool frees a fifth of the planning team's time. One planner retires next month. What does the course suggest?
a: Hire a replacement quickly to keep the team at full strength
b: Wait a year before deciding anything about the team
c: Give the remaining planners more training on the tool
d: Do not replace the planner: that turns freed time into money
explanation: Freed time becomes money only through a decision, such as not replacing a leaver. Hiring a replacement quietly reabsorbs the gain.

stem: How does the course recommend framing an AI gain when presenting it to plant teams?
a: As headcount the plant will be able to remove
b: As throughput: the same team producing more
c: As a percentage cut in the plant's labor cost
d: As hours each worker saves per week with the tool
explanation: Frame gains as throughput: the same team producing more. It matches where the value usually sits and does not turn the team against the tool.

stem: Volume fell 15% after go-live and costs dropped. What stops your gains claim from counting the downturn?
a: Reporting only the first good month after go-live
b: A baseline normalized for volume and mix
c: Comparing against last year's best quarter
d: Keeping finance out of the review until the end
explanation: A gain is a difference against a baseline that moves with volume, mix and price: normalized baseline = baseline rate × actual volume, per family.

stem: Machine hours are freed in a plant that is not sold out. How should those hours be valued?
a: At the plant's full cost per machine-hour, overheads included
b: At the contribution margin of extra sales
c: At avoided variable cost, or via a structural decision
d: At the list price the vendor quotes for capacity
explanation: Contribution margin applies only when extra volume can actually be sold. Otherwise freed hours are worth avoided variable cost, or a structural move such as closing a shift, which management decides.

stem: Your team lists 'better visibility for planners' as a gain but cannot link it to any P&L line. How should the gains case treat it?
a: As a soft gain, valued at a share of planner salaries
b: As the main gain, since visibility drives all the others
c: As no gain until it branches to a financial line
d: As a gain counted once users confirm it in a survey
explanation: The gains tree runs from operational lever to physical effect to financial line. No branch to a P&L line, no gain.

stem: A tool shortens changeovers. Which chain is a complete branch of the gains tree?
a: Shorter changeovers, a higher OEE score on the plant dashboard
b: Shorter changeovers, happier planners and better team morale on site
c: Shorter changeovers, fewer planner hours spent in spreadsheets
d: Shorter changeovers, more bottleneck output, margin on extra sales
explanation: A complete branch links lever, physical effect and financial line. A better OEE score is a physical effect that stops before reaching the P&L.

stem: Demand at Polymex Industries is strongly seasonal. Which baseline period does the course call for?
a: The 3 months just before go-live
b: 12 rolling months
c: The 6 months of high season
d: The best single month of last year
explanation: With seasonality, the baseline covers 12 rolling months, never fewer than 6. A season-only window bakes the seasonal effect into the claimed gain.

stem: Halfway through, the plant asks to add two new lines to the measured scope of the gains claim. What does baseline discipline require?
a: Keep the frozen, named perimeter; treat the new lines separately
b: Add them, and use the plant-wide average as their baseline
c: Add them, since a larger scope makes the claim more credible
d: Restart the whole baseline from scratch, including all of the lines
explanation: Baseline discipline means a frozen, named perimeter. Changing scope mid-way makes before and after incomparable; new lines need their own agreed baseline.

stem: Resin prices fell 20% after go-live, cutting material costs. How should the gains claim treat this drop?
a: Count it, since it happened after the tool went live
b: Count half of it, as a compromise with finance
c: Normalize for price, so the drop is not claimed as a gain
d: Count it in full unless the controller can prove it came from elsewhere
explanation: The baseline is normalized for volume, mix and price. A market price drop is not caused by the tool, and claiming it destroys credibility with finance.

stem: Of the four gain types, which carries the lightest burden of proof with finance?
a: Cost-out, such as an invoice that disappears
b: Revenue protection, such as a customer kept
c: Capacity release, such as machine hours freed
d: Cash release, such as inventory reduced
explanation: Cost-out is the easiest to validate. Capacity release needs the sold-out fork, cash release counts once, and revenue protection faces the most skepticism.

stem: Your gains case says the tool prevented the loss of a major customer. What will finance need before counting it?
a: The sales team's estimate of how likely the loss was
b: A customer satisfaction survey run after go-live
c: The project team's model of churn risk across all customer accounts
d: Contractual evidence, such as penalty clauses
explanation: Revenue protection carries the highest skepticism and needs contractual evidence. Estimates, surveys and models are not proof that revenue was at risk.

stem: Your plant is sold out and the tool frees bottleneck hours. Before valuing them at contribution margin, what must you obtain?
a: Confirmation from sales that the extra volume can be sold
b: The vendor's benchmark for freed capacity at similar sites
c: The full cost per machine-hour from the cost accounts
d: Agreement from the operators to work the freed hours
explanation: Capacity release becomes money at contribution margin only when sales confirm the extra volume can be sold. Full cost and vendor benchmarks do not prove it.

stem: A new scheduler and a lean program both claim the same overtime reduction. What rule applies?
a: Each program counts the full reduction in its own case, as both helped
b: Count it once across both, allocated as agreed with finance
c: The program that started first counts all of it
d: Neither counts it, since attribution is impossible
explanation: Counting rules forbid double counting with other initiatives. The saving exists once; finance must see one figure, however it is shared.

stem: Three months after go-live, the team reports the annualized run-rate as this year's savings. What is wrong?
a: Nothing, since run-rate is the standard way to report
b: Run-rate should be reported net of the vendor discount
c: The run-rate should be based on the best single week
d: Run-rate is not realized gain; report the two separately
explanation: Counting rules separate run-rate from realized gains. Annualizing three good months and calling it this year's savings overstates what finance will see.

stem: The gains case shows €1M saved but leaves out €300K of software and integration costs. What does finance expect?
a: Gains shown net of the cost to achieve them
b: Gains shown gross, with costs left to the IT budget
c: Costs shown only in the year the project ends
d: Gains rounded up to offset the missing costs
explanation: Counting rules distinguish gross from net of the cost to achieve. Finance expects the net figure, here €700K, not gross savings with costs parked elsewhere.

stem: When should the baseline be agreed with the plant controller?
a: Once the pilot shows promising early results
b: In week 1, before any software runs
c: At go-live, when the first real data arrives
d: At year end, when the accounts are closed
explanation: The baseline is co-built with the controller in week 1, before any software runs. Agreed later, it is negotiated around results and gains leak before go-live.

stem: At the start of a deployment, what do you agree in writing with the controller?
a: The model choice, the hosting and the licence terms
b: The target gain and the bonus the project team earns if it is reached
c: Metric, formula, data source, normalization and sign-off rule
d: The go-live date, the training plan and the user list
explanation: The finance protocol fixes in writing the metric, formula, data source, normalization, review cadence and sign-off threshold, so the gain is not argued afterwards.

stem: Your team and the controller compute slightly different gains for the quarter. Which figure gets announced?
a: The project team's, since it knows the tool best
b: The average of the two, to be fair to both sides
c: The controller's, from finance's own spreadsheet
d: The higher of the two, if the team can justify it
explanation: The gain is announced by finance's spreadsheet, not yours. Differences go back to the agreed formula, not into a compromise figure.

stem: Who should own the capture of gains after go-live?
a: The FDE team that built and deployed the tool
b: A client-side owner with a mandate over the decisions
c: The vendor's customer success manager for the account
d: The IT department that runs the system day to day
explanation: Capture needs an owner on the client side with a formal mandate on the gains and authority over the decisions behind them. Builders and IT cannot take those decisions.

stem: Alex is named gains owner but cannot change shift patterns or overtime rules. Why is capture at risk?
a: Alex should have been chosen from the project team that built the tool
b: Shift patterns have little to do with captured gains
c: Gains owners should report to IT rather than operations
d: Alex lacks the authority to take the decisions behind the gains
explanation: A gains owner needs a formal mandate and the authority to take the decisions behind the gains. A title without that authority leaves freed capacity unconverted.

stem: The tool proposes better sequences, but supervisors keep scheduling the old way. Where is value leaking?
a: Before go-live, through a baseline nobody agreed
b: In the numbers, as KPIs and claims drift apart
c: On the floor, as decisions still run on habit
d: In the model, through errors in its sequencing
explanation: Gains leak before go-live, on the floor and in the numbers. Here the tool works but decisions still follow habit, so the gain never reaches the P&L.

stem: Long changeovers once limited Polymex Industries to two product launches a year. The tool removed that constraint. What follows?
a: Reopen the two-launch rule, since its constraint is gone
b: Keep the rule, as it is part of the operating plan
c: Wait several years before reviewing any of the plant's planning rules
d: Count the removed constraint as an immediate gain
explanation: Operating parameters treated as fixed should be reopened once the constraint behind them is gone. Removing the constraint is not yet a gain; using it is.

stem: Replanning used to take a day, so the plant reschedules weekly. The tool now replans in minutes. What should the manager do?
a: Keep the weekly cadence, since the floor is used to it
b: Revisit the weekly cadence, set when replanning was slow
c: Replan every few minutes, whenever the tool allows it
d: Report the minutes saved per replan as the project gain
explanation: Rescheduling cadence is a parameter set by an old constraint. Once replanning is fast, reopen it; replanning constantly would unsettle the floor.

stem: Changeovers take 10,000 hours a year and a tool cuts them by 30%. Sold-out plant, €100 contribution per hour, software €100K a year. Net annual gain?
explanation: 3,000 freed hours × €100 = €300K gross, minus €100K of software = €200K net. €300K forgets the cost to achieve; €700K values the remaining hours; €1M forgets the 30%.

stem: Inventory falls by €2M after deployment. How should this appear in the gains case?
a: As €2M of recurring savings every year
b: One-time €2M cash release, plus recurring carrying-cost savings
c: Not at all, because inventory never appears anywhere on the P&L
d: As €400K of savings a year over five years
explanation: Cash release counts once as cash, and recurringly only as carrying cost. Presenting the one-time figure as annual savings destroys credibility with finance.

stem: Sold-out plant. A tool frees 2,000 bottleneck hours a year, but the backlog absorbs only 500 more. At €200 contribution per hour, how much is valued at contribution margin?
explanation: Contribution margin applies only to sellable hours, capped by the backlog: 500 × €200 = €100K. €400K values all 2,000 hours as if they could be sold.

stem: Plant not sold out. A tool frees 1,000 machine hours. Variable cost €40 per hour, full cost €150, contribution €120. Absent any structural decision, what are they worth?
explanation: When freed hours cannot be sold, they are worth avoided variable cost: 1,000 × €40 = €40K. Full cost and contribution margin overstate the gain.
flags: reviewer note: relies on stem phrase

stem: In a sold-out plant, a tool frees hours on a machine that is not the bottleneck. How should those hours be valued?
a: At contribution margin, since the plant is sold out
b: At full cost per hour, including the overheads
c: At most at avoided variable cost, as output cannot rise
d: At the bottleneck's hourly rate, since all hours are alike
explanation: Freed capacity is worth contribution margin only when it becomes sellable output. Off the bottleneck, plant output does not rise, so at most variable cost is avoided.

stem: Your gains case values freed hours at full cost per hour, overheads included. Why will finance reject it?
a: Full cost must first be adjusted for inflation
b: Freed hours should be valued at list price instead
c: Only direct labor cost can be counted in a gains case
d: Overheads do not fall when machine hours are freed
explanation: Valuing freed hours at full cost is a classic error: overheads stay. Value at contribution margin when sellable, otherwise at avoided variable cost.

stem: Six months in, the order backlog has shrunk and no longer absorbs all freed hours. What happens to the capacity valuation?
a: Hours beyond the backlog drop to avoided variable cost
b: Nothing, since the valuation was fixed and signed off at go-live
c: All freed hours drop to zero value from that point
d: The plant should now value the hours at full cost
explanation: Contribution margin is capped by the order backlog. Hours that can no longer be sold are worth avoided variable cost, so the case must be revalued.

stem: What marks a strong gains case, under the course's base, low and high case rule?
a: Its high case is at least double its base case
b: It still holds up in its own low case
c: Its base case matches the vendor's benchmark
d: Its figures come from a single, simple case
explanation: Base, low and high cases name the driving assumption, and a strong case survives its own low case. A wide upside proves nothing about robustness.

stem: You present base, low and high cases to the CFO. What must each case make explicit?
a: The vendor's guarantee behind each figure
b: The names of the people who built each case
c: The software cost alone, since gains are uncertain
d: The driving assumption that moves the result
explanation: Each scenario names its driving assumption, so finance can judge which belief the result rests on and test it.

stem: Your base case is strong but the low case shows a net loss. What should you do before the steering committee?
a: Present only the base case to keep the message simple
b: Average the three cases and present that single figure to the committee
c: Treat the case as fragile and rework scope or the key assumption
d: Drop the low case as unrealistically pessimistic
explanation: A strong case survives its own low case. A loss in the low case means the result hangs on one assumption; hiding or averaging it misleads finance.

stem: Your result swings mostly with how much extra volume sales can place. How should low and high cases be built?
a: Vary that volume assumption and name it as the driver
b: Apply plus or minus 10% to the final figure for each of the two cases
c: Vary the software cost, which is easiest to estimate
d: Move every input by the same percentage at once
explanation: Low and high cases flex the driving assumption and name it. A flat percentage on the total hides what the result actually depends on.

stem: Bottom-up hours × rates gives €2M a year; top-down from the P&L gives €1.8M. What next?
a: Find the error first, since the methods disagree
b: Present only the higher figure, since it is more detailed
c: Present it: the two methods agree closely enough
d: Build a third estimate before showing anything
explanation: When two independent estimates land within 20 to 30% of each other, present the number. A 10% gap is well inside that range.

stem: Your bottom-up estimate is €3M a year; the top-down estimate from the P&L is €1M. What do you do?
a: Present the average of €2M as a compromise
b: Present the bottom-up figure, as it is more detailed
c: Present both and let finance choose between them
d: Find the error before presenting any figure
explanation: Triangulated estimates should agree within 20 to 30%. A threefold gap means one method is wrong; averaging just hides the error.

stem: What does triangulating a gains estimate mean?
a: Asking three people from finance to check the same spreadsheet
b: Building the same number a second, independent way
c: Presenting base, low and high cases side by side
d: Comparing the estimate with a vendor's benchmark
explanation: Triangulation rebuilds the number independently, for example top-down from the P&L against bottom-up hours × rates. Scenarios test assumptions, not the method.

stem: Two estimates of the gain agree within 5%, but both start from the same hours-saved figure. Why is that weak?
a: They are not independent, so agreement proves little
b: A 5% gap is too close, since real estimates always differ by more
c: Hours saved should never be used in a gains case
d: Finance accepts only top-down estimates of gains
explanation: Triangulation needs a second, independent route to the number. Two methods sharing the same key input repeat its error rather than test it.

stem: One-time cost €300K. Net gains run at €50K a month for the first two months of ramp, then €100K a month. Payback?
a: 2 months
b: 3 months
c: 4 months
d: 6 months
explanation: The ramp yields €100K in two months; the remaining €200K takes two more at €100K, so payback is 4 months. Ignoring the ramp gives 3.

stem: Your payback divides one-time cost by the full run-rate from day one. What does this miss?
a: The vendor's discount on the second year
b: The full cost of the plant's overheads
c: The yearly depreciation of the plant's existing machines and tooling
d: The ramp: months of lower gains before steady state
explanation: Payback is one-time cost ÷ monthly net run-rate, including the ramp. Assuming full run-rate from day one flatters it.

stem: A tool costs €360K one-time plus €30K a month to run, and saves €90K a month from day one. Payback?
a: 4 months
b: 6 months
c: 9 months
d: 12 months
explanation: Payback uses the net run-rate: €90K − €30K = €60K a month, so €360K ÷ €60K = 6 months. Four months forgets the running cost.

stem: A pilot on the plant's newest, best-run line shows a 25% gain. How should you extrapolate to the whole site?
a: Apply 25% to every line, as the pilot proved it
b: Raise it, since older lines have more room to improve
c: Discount it: pilot lines are rarely representative
d: Wait for the vendor to publish a site-wide figure
explanation: Pilot machines are rarely representative. Results from the best-run line need adjusting for the conditions of the other lines before they size a rollout.

stem: Why do pilot results often overstate what a rollout will deliver?
a: Models lose accuracy as more users join the system
b: Pilot machines are picked for good data and keen teams
c: Rollouts usually run on a cheaper, less capable version of the tool
d: Finance applies looser rules to pilots than to plants
explanation: Pilot selection bias: pilots go where data is clean and teams are willing, so they are rarely representative of the machines a rollout reaches.

stem: Sam must pick machines for a pilot whose results will size a rollout case. What keeps the case honest?
a: Include typical machines, not only the best documented
b: Choose the best machines, to prove what the tool can do at its best
c: Choose the worst machines, to show the largest gain
d: Let the vendor choose, as it knows the tool best
explanation: Pilot machines are rarely representative, so a pilot that sizes a rollout should include typical machines. Best-case or worst-case picks both bias the number.

stem: A tool cuts scrap of purchased raw material. Which line of the P&L improves first?
a: Revenue, through higher selling prices
b: Inventory, as a one-time cash release
c: Sales and admin overheads, below gross margin
d: Cost of goods sold, lifting gross margin
explanation: Material lost as scrap is part of cost of goods sold, so less scrap lowers it and raises gross margin. Inventory sits on the balance sheet, not the P&L.

stem: Fewer invoice disputes mean customers pay 20 days sooner. How does this show up in the gains case?
a: A recurring yearly saving equal to the receivables drop
b: Higher revenue in the year of go-live
c: Lower receivables: mainly a one-time cash release
d: Lower cost of goods sold from next year
explanation: Receivables are working capital. Collecting sooner releases cash once; only the financing cost saved recurs.

stem: A line delivers the same output in 500 fewer hours. Which cost actually falls?
a: Depreciation charged each year on the line's machines and tooling
b: Energy and consumables used per running hour
c: The plant manager's salary
d: Rent on the plant building
explanation: Fewer running hours cut variable costs such as energy and consumables. Depreciation, salaries and rent are fixed and stay unless a structural decision is taken.

stem: What separates gross margin from EBITDA?
a: Gross margin already deducts interest and taxes for the year
b: EBITDA leaves out cost of goods sold entirely
c: They are the same figure under two different names
d: EBITDA also deducts operating overheads such as sales and admin
explanation: Gross margin is revenue minus cost of goods sold. EBITDA further deducts operating overheads, before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization.

stem: How is contribution margin per unit calculated?
a: Price minus variable cost per unit
b: Price minus full cost, overheads included
c: Revenue minus EBITDA, divided by volume
d: Variable cost plus a share of fixed cost
explanation: Contribution margin is price minus variable cost: what each extra unit adds to cover fixed costs and profit. Deducting overheads gives a full-cost margin instead.

stem: Last year a line used 25,000 MWh for 12,500 tonnes. This year it used 18,000 MWh for 10,000 tonnes. Volume-normalized saving?
explanation: Baseline rate 2 MWh per tonne × 10,000 tonnes = 20,000 MWh normalized; 20,000 − 18,000 = 2,000 MWh. 7,000 counts the volume drop as a gain.

stem: The product mix shifted toward a family with long cycle times. Why normalize the baseline per family rather than plant-wide?
a: Finance accepts figures only at the level of each individual product family
b: Plant-wide figures are too large for finance to audit
c: A plant-wide rate hides shifts between families with different rates
d: Per-family figures nearly always show a larger gain
explanation: Normalized baseline = baseline rate × actual volume, per product family. One plant-wide rate turns a mix shift into a false gain or a false loss.

stem: Baseline cost per unit: family A €10, family B €20. This year: 1,000 A and 500 B, at a total cost of €18,000. Normalized gain?
explanation: Normalized baseline: 1,000 × €10 + 500 × €20 = €20,000, against €18,000 actual, a €2,000 gain. €4,500 wrongly uses a €15 average rate.

stem: A product family launched after go-live has no baseline rate. How should its results enter the gains claim?
a: Use the plant-wide average rate of all other families as its baseline
b: Count all of its output as gain, since it is new
c: Use its rate in the first month after launch
d: Leave it out unless finance agrees a rate in writing
explanation: The baseline covers a frozen, named perimeter agreed with finance. A family without a baseline rate stays outside the claim until the controller agrees one.

stem: Volume rose 20% after go-live and total cost rose 10%. The plant says costs went up, so the tool has no gain. What is right?
a: Agree: costs rose, so there is no gain to claim
b: Compare with last year's total cost, unadjusted for volume or mix
c: Compare cost with baseline rate × actual volume, per family
d: Exclude the year, since volume changed too much
explanation: Normalize: cost should be compared with baseline rate × actual volume, per family. Here cost grew less than volume, which can reveal a real gain.

stem: Using the tool's data, procurement wins a one-off €200K rebate from a supplier. How is it counted?
a: Once, as a one-time gain, not as an annual saving
b: As €200K of savings every year from now on
c: Spread as €40K a year over five years
d: Not at all, since procurement negotiated it
explanation: Counting rules separate recurring from one-time gains. A one-off rebate counts once; presenting it as annual savings overstates the case.

stem: Your bottom-up case puts 70% of the value in direct labor savings. What should you check first?
a: Nothing more, since labor is normally the main source of value
b: Whether working capital, speed, quality or capex gains were missed
c: Whether more headcount could be cut to raise the total
d: Whether the labor rates include enough of the plant's overhead
explanation: Direct labor is usually at most about a quarter of the value. A labor-heavy case has probably missed working capital, speed to revenue, quality or deferred capex.

stem: Your scheduler frees 1,500 bottleneck hours a year in a sold-out plant. Sales confirms orders for 600 of them. How do you value the other 900?
a: At contribution margin, since the plant is sold out today
b: At the plant's full cost per hour, since the capacity is real
c: At avoided variable cost, unless management takes a structural decision
d: At contribution margin, discounted by half for uncertainty
explanation: Contribution margin applies only to hours that sales can fill, capped by the order backlog. Hours beyond it are worth avoided variable cost, or a structural move such as closing a shift, which management decides.

stem: A plant runs at 64% of capacity. Your tool frees 2,000 hours on one line. The plant manager asks what they are worth. What is the honest answer?
a: Their contribution margin, since output could now rise
b: Only the overtime, energy or outsourcing they avoid, or a shift closed
c: Their full cost per hour, since fixed costs now spread over fewer running hours
d: Nothing at all, because freed hours never reach the P&L
explanation: With spare capacity and flat demand, nobody buys the extra output. Freed hours are worth the variable cost they avoid, or a structural decision management takes. Zero is too strong: avoided overtime is real money.

stem: Late deliveries are costing the plant orders, and your tool lifts on-time delivery. What must you have before counting the contribution of orders kept?
a: A customer survey showing satisfaction is rising
b: On-time delivery held above 95% for a full quarter, as measured by the plant
c: The plant manager's estimate of the volume at risk
d: Sales naming the orders at risk, backed by contracts or emails
explanation: Revenue protection carries the heaviest burden of proof: finance counts it only when sales names the orders, with contractual or written evidence. A better service level alone proves no euro was kept.

stem: Sales says two accounts would take 6% more volume with shorter lead times, but nothing is in writing. How should your gains case treat that volume?
a: Outside the base case, as an assumption sales must confirm by a date
b: In the base case, since the sales director said it out loud
c: As validated revenue, from the day lead times start to fall
d: Left out entirely, and not mentioned to the sponsor at all
explanation: An unconfirmed sale is an assumption: log it with an owner and a date, and keep it out of the base case until sales confirms it. Hiding it loses a real upside; counting it now overstates the case.

stem: Your low and high cases are simply the base case minus and plus 10%. The CFO is not convinced. Why?
a: The range should be wider, about 25%, to look prudent
b: Each case should move one named assumption, not a fixed margin
c: The high case should already include the rollout to other sites
d: A CFO wants one number, so ranges only create confusion
explanation: Low, base and high cases are each driven by a named assumption, such as volume sales can place or the gain on typical machines. A symmetric margin shows no understanding of what moves the result.

stem: Your cost-out case still pays if the pilot gain halves. Your capacity case turns negative if demand softens. Which do you lead with at the steering committee?
a: The capacity case, since its base case is the larger one
b: The sum of the two, presented as one program figure
c: Neither, until both have run for a full year on site
d: The cost-out case, since it survives its own low case
explanation: A strong case survives its own low case. The capacity case depends on demand that may not come, so it is a condition to state, not the headline. Waiting a year forfeits a case that already holds.

stem: Planners say yield on the problem families is 'about 20% lower', but nobody measures it. Your sizing rests on that gap. What do you do?
a: Use 20% in the base case, since the planners know the floor
b: Drop the yield effect and size only the changeover hours
c: Measure it early, and until then treat it as a named range
d: Use the ERP's standard rates, which the controller trusts
explanation: An estimate nobody has measured is an assumption: carry it as a range, name it as a driver, and plan how to measure it. Saying what you do not know, and how you will find out, is what a steering committee expects.

stem: Bottom-up, hours freed × contribution gives €1.2M a year. Top-down, the share of the P&L line the lever can touch gives €1.0M. What next?
a: Present it, showing both paths and the gap between them
b: Average the two and present €1.1M as the single figure
c: Keep working on both paths until the two agree within about 5%
d: Present the bottom-up figure, as it is more detailed
explanation: Two independent paths within 20 to 30% of each other support the order of magnitude, so present it and show both. Chasing a 5% match wastes time; averaging hides the method.

stem: Your case is hours saved × contribution per hour. Which second estimate is a real triangulation?
a: The same hours saved, recomputed with the controller's own hourly rates
b: The pilot result on three machines, scaled to the whole site
c: A vendor benchmark of gains at plants of a similar size
d: Top-down: the share of the affected P&L line the lever can move
explanation: Triangulation builds the number a second, independent way. Reusing the same hours with other rates repeats the first path's main assumption, so agreement would prove little.

stem: One-time cost €200K. Net gains run at €25K a month for the first four months, then €50K a month. What is the payback?
a: 4 months
b: 5 months
c: 6 months
d: 8 months
explanation: Four ramp months return €100K; the remaining €100K takes two months at €50K, so 6 months. Dividing by the full run-rate gives 4 and ignores the ramp.

stem: In month four, gains run at €40K a month. The sponsor wants to tell the board 'about €480K this year'. What do you advise?
a: Fine, as long as finance signed the month-four figure
b: Fine, since annualizing a monthly run-rate is common reporting practice
c: Report €480K now and correct it at the year-end close
d: Call €480K a run-rate, and report what is realized separately
explanation: €40K × 12 is a run-rate, not this year's gain: the months before go-live and the ramp earned less. Run-rate and realized are always stated separately, even when the monthly figure is signed.

stem: Your net gain deducts the software and your team's fees. The controller says the figure is still not net. What did you most likely leave out?
a: The depreciation of the machines that the new tool now schedules
b: The time the client's own people spend on the project
c: The revenue lost while the system was being deployed
d: The vendor's margin built into the software price
explanation: The cost to achieve covers software, the deployment and the client's time: planners, IT and the controller. Depreciation of existing machines does not change with the project.

stem: Your pilot ran on the three machines with the best data and the keenest crew. The rollout covers 14 machines. How do you size the rollout?
a: Scale the pilot gain to all 14 machines, exactly as measured
b: Discount the pilot gain and make it the low case's driver
c: Repeat the pilot on the same three machines to confirm it first
d: Replace the pilot result with a vendor's average gain
explanation: Pilot machines are chosen for clean data and keen teams, so they are rarely representative. Discount the gain for typical machines and name it as the assumption that drives the range.
source: Doctrine, value, ROI, validated gains and capture

stem: Your case shows €1M of stock reduction plus €200K a year of carrying cost saved, summed as €1.2M a year. What is wrong?
a: Carrying cost should not count, since stock is not on the P&L
b: Stock reduction should be spread over five years as savings
c: The cash comes once; only the carrying cost recurs each year
d: Nothing, if the controller agrees the carrying-cost rate
explanation: Inventory releases cash once, in the year stock goes down, and saves carrying cost every year after. Adding the two into one annual figure counts the same euros twice.

stem: Your case values fewer changeover hours at contribution margin, and separately adds the overtime those changeovers used to cause. What will the controller say?
a: The overtime is a symptom of the changeovers: count it once
b: The overtime belongs in the case, as a cost-out line
c: The changeover hours should be valued at full cost instead
d: The two lines stand, as long as each one is normalized for volume and mix
explanation: Overtime is usually a symptom of changeovers and late plans. Counting both the freed hours and the overtime they caused adds the same euro twice; choose one valuation through the demand fork.

stem: Price €1,700 a tonne, variable cost €1,300, full cost €1,600. A sold-out line makes 1,000 more tonnes that sales has placed. What are they worth?
explanation: A tonne is worth its contribution margin: €1,700 − €1,300 = €400 × 1,000 = €400K. Price minus full cost gives €100K and wrongly charges fixed costs that do not move with volume.

stem: At a plant with flat demand, the manager says higher OEE will cut cost per tonne and so lift EBIT. What is your view?
a: Right: a lower cost per tonne always reaches EBIT within the same year
b: Right, provided the OEE gain is measured on the bottleneck line
c: A paper gain only, unless the extra output sells or cash costs fall
d: Wrong: OEE has no link with cost, only with delivery
explanation: Depreciation and salaried staff do not move when machines run longer. Spreading them over more unsold tonnes lowers unit cost on paper without changing EBIT; money comes from sales or avoided variable cost.
