stem: Your baseline period includes a week when a line was down for planned maintenance. What should the validation protocol say?
a: Nothing: such weeks average out over the baseline period
b: The rule for such weeks, written before any result is known
c: That the FDE team decides each such week case by case
d: That such weeks are dropped whenever they happen to lower the gain
explanation: The controller must run the protocol without you, including what to do with abnormal weeks. A rule fixed in advance stops anyone choosing exclusions after seeing the result.

stem: Mix moved toward a family that costs twice as much per tonne. Plant-wide cost per tonne rose 5%, and the plant manager says the tool failed. What do you do?
a: Accept it: cost per tonne is the metric the plant reports
b: Recompute the baseline as each family's rate × actual volume
c: Remove the expensive family from the perimeter after the fact
d: Compare against the best month of the baseline year, when the mix was similar
explanation: A plant-wide rate hides shifts between families with different rates. The normalized baseline is baseline rate × actual volume, per family; changing the perimeter afterwards breaks baseline discipline.
source: Doctrine, value, ROI, validated gains and capture

stem: Your pipeline gives cleaner output data than the ERP export finance uses today. Which should the baseline use?
a: Your pipeline, since its data quality is higher
b: An average of the two sources, so that neither side can dispute it
c: The system finance already trusts, with its gaps written down
d: Whichever source shows the more conservative baseline
explanation: The baseline uses the system finance already trusts, owned by the client, with its known gaps documented in the protocol. A gain built on your own pipeline is one the controller cannot compute without you.

stem: Another team's Verifier, playing the controller, cannot tell from your protocol which file to open or who sends it. What does that show?
a: The protocol is not finished: it must run without you
b: The Verifier needs a short briefing from your team first
c: The file name belongs in the steering deck, not the protocol
d: The detail can wait until the first monthly review
explanation: A gain exists when the client's controller computes it without you. If the protocol does not say which file, from whom, it fails the controller test; a briefing only hides the gap.

stem: Your protocol says the gain becomes official 'once results are consistently good'. What should the sign-off trigger say instead?
a: That the sponsor approves each monthly figure in writing
b: A confidence interval computed from your team's model
c: A fixed date after which the gain is assumed to hold
d: A value, and how long it must hold, such as three months
explanation: The sign-off trigger is a value and a duration agreed in week one, so the controller knows exactly which number, held how long, makes it official. Sponsor approval is not finance validation.

stem: The group controller says: 'I have never seen a scheduling gain I could find in my numbers.' What is your first move?
a: Show the gains other clients reached with similar tools
b: Ask the sponsor to overrule the controller on the gain
c: Send weekly reports from the tool, so that the gain becomes visible to finance
d: Build the baseline and formula with the controller, from their data
explanation: The controller's doubt is the requirement: co-build the baseline, formula and sign-off rule in week one, from the data finance trusts. Reports from your own tool are exactly what was never found in the numbers.

stem: Your scheduling project pushes on-time delivery. Which measure is a guardrail on its scorecard?
a: Plans published from the system each week
b: Scrap and changeovers per shift
c: Answer time to a customer's change request
d: Quoted lead time on new orders
explanation: A guardrail is what must not get worse while you push the outcome: on-time delivery bought with extra changeovers is paid in scrap. Plans published is adoption; answer time is a driver; lead time is an outcome.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture

stem: The team proposes 'parser accuracy above 98%' as the project's headline success measure. What is wrong with it?
a: It describes the system, not what the plant or customer notices
b: 98% is too low a bar for a parser running in production
c: It should be computed by the controller, not by the team
d: Accuracy should be measured on a sample, not on every message
explanation: Good is defined by what the client would notice. Parser accuracy belongs in the eval set; the headline measure is an outcome such as on-time delivery or quoted lead time.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture

stem: Baseline on-time delivery is 84%; the best week last quarter was 91%; the solver says a perfect plan gives 97%. Where should the target sit?
a: At 86%, two points above the baseline, to be safe
b: At 91%, since the best week proves it can be done
c: Between 91% and 97%, with a date and an owner
d: At 97%, since the solver proves it is reachable
explanation: The target sits between best demonstrated and entitlement, with a number, a date and an owner. Entitlement assumes a perfect plan; two points over baseline may be lost in weekly noise.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture

stem: Weekly on-time delivery moves about two points with nothing changing. The draft charter promises one point of improvement. What do you change?
a: Nothing: one point a week adds up over a year
b: Measure monthly instead, so that the weekly noise disappears from view
c: Aim higher, or measure something closer to the cause
d: Ask the controller to smooth the weekly figures
explanation: A gain smaller than the weekly noise cannot be seen, so nobody can sign it. Size the target above the noise, or pick a driver measure closer to the cause that moves visibly.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture

stem: Week 6: you find the scrap baseline counts regrind twice, so the gain shown to the CFO is a third too high. Steering is on Friday. What do you do?
a: Tell the sponsor and controller within a day, with the corrected figure
b: Correct it quietly in the next monthly report
c: Wait for Friday and present the correction to the whole committee
d: Keep the figure, since the trend in scrap is still right
explanation: Announce the error first, with the corrected number and what it changes. Trust lost by a correction comes back; trust lost by a cover-up does not. Waiting for Friday lets the CFO hear it in a meeting.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: You bring the planning system to a second plant running at 64% of capacity. Its planner shows no interest. What is the likely reason?
a: She has not yet seen the gains measured at the first plant
b: She needs more training on the system before she adopts it
c: She wins little from a better plan when lines are half empty
d: Her plant manager has not yet made use of the system mandatory for her
explanation: Each actor must be able to say what they win. In a plant short of orders a better plan moves little, so the first plant's product may be the wrong first product there; start from that plant's own problem.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: The group COO wants one gain figure for the four-plant rollout, computed by your central team. What do you propose?
a: One figure, computed centrally with a shared group method
b: The first plant's gain, multiplied by the number of plants
c: A group figure from the ERP, signed by the group CFO alone
d: Gains each plant's controller measures, then added up
explanation: What counts as a gain belongs to the controller, and each plant has its own baseline and perimeter. The COO gets gains a controller can measure plant by plant; a central figure is the team's model again.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: Your kickoff document for the client's executive committee has a target, scope and roles. What must it also set for each gate?
a: A measurable condition that stops the project, agreed now
b: A budget reserve to extend the phase if it runs late
c: The list of features the team will deliver by the end of that phase
d: The user satisfaction score the phase should reach
explanation: Kill criteria are written on day one, one per gate, while nobody is attached to the solution yet. About 30% of initiatives fail; a stop at a gate keeps the account, a zombie project loses it.

stem: At week 4, the backtest shows changeovers explain a fifth of the delivery loss; the charter's kill criterion said a third. The sponsor wants to go on. What do you do?
a: Extend the phase by four more weeks, to gather more data on the losses
b: Lower the threshold, since a fifth is still material
c: Continue, and raise it at the next steering committee
d: Take the stop to the steering committee, written up as a result
explanation: The kill criterion was agreed before anyone was attached, so it holds. A kill is a result: write it up and send it to the controller like a gain. Moving the threshold after the fact empties the charter.

stem: A use case would save €150K a year; capturing it costs €100K a year in software and people. The sponsor likes it. What do you advise?
a: Look elsewhere: it is not worth ten times its cost
b: Go ahead, but only after a pilot on the best line
c: Go ahead, since the net gain is positive from year one
d: Go ahead if the vendor cuts the software price
explanation: A problem worth solving is worth at least ten times what it costs to capture. A thin positive margin disappears with the first delay or the low case, and leaves no room for the change it demands.

stem: What best distinguishes a Forward Deployed Engineer from a consultant?
a: The FDE produces more detailed and better-researched written recommendations
b: The FDE also sells software licences alongside the work
c: The FDE stays accountable for running systems and measured gains
d: The FDE works remotely, close to the product team
explanation: Consultants deliver recommendations. FDEs deliver production code, running systems and euro gains, and the same person owns the outcome from scoping to steady state.

stem: Why are the first three months of an engagement budgeted as discovery rather than delivery?
a: Data and organizational problems surface only once AI runs on real data
b: Enterprise software licences usually take about three months to activate
c: Regulation requires a three-month audit before any AI
d: It increases the number of billable days per client
explanation: Data quality issues appear at inference, and organizational change slides relative to technical plans. Budgeting discovery up front avoids a delay that was always going to happen.

stem: Your AI pilot impressed in the demo, then stalled once rolled out in the plant. Where does the course say enterprise AI usually fails?
a: The model was not powerful enough for industrial work
b: In the last mile: legacy data and changing how people work
c: The demo budget was too small to build a convincing prototype
d: The cloud provider could not scale to plant volumes
explanation: Deployment, not models, is the bottleneck. Value is lost where data sits in legacy systems and people must change how they work, which a stronger model does not fix.

stem: Your plant wants an AI scheduling tool. Where should the engineers building it spend most of their time?
a: At headquarters, close to the IT department and its architects
b: With the vendor's product team, refining the core features
c: Remotely, working from written requirements gathered by managers
d: In the plant, next to the planners and quality leads
explanation: Engineers in the plant see the real constraint, the workarounds and the data in people's heads, and can ship in weeks. Requirements written at a distance miss what planners actually do.

stem: A partner offers engineers at a daily rate who take tasks from your IT backlog. What separates this from an FDE engagement?
a: The FDE owns a business outcome in production
b: The FDE brings a larger team of junior developers
c: The FDE writes more code per day than contractors do
d: The FDE reports to the vendor's sales team, not to IT
explanation: Staffing supplies capacity. An FDE is accountable for production code, running systems and measured euro gains: the difference is ownership of the outcome, not the volume of work.

stem: Two months into an AI engagement, your team is still cleaning data and mapping workarounds, with no gains yet. How should you read this?
a: The team is failing and should be replaced quickly
b: The scope was too ambitious and should be cut in half before month three
c: As expected: early months are discovery and stabilization
d: The data is unusable, so the engagement should stop
explanation: The first three months are discovery and stabilization, because data and organizational problems only surface on real data. Gains are expected after that, not in week one.

stem: Your deployment is two weeks late. What does the no-surprises rule require?
a: Work weekends and report once you are back on track
b: Wait for the next monthly steering committee to raise it
c: Quietly reduce the scope to protect the original date
d: Tell the sponsor now, with the cause and a recovery plan
explanation: Bad news travels fast. A sponsor who learns of a slip late stops trusting the project; one who learns early can help remove the cause.

stem: Your FDE has found a high-value scheduling problem at Polymex Industries. In the FDE loop, what comes next?
a: Build fast with the systems and data that already exist
b: Write a full specification and send it out to tender
c: Wait for the new data warehouse project to finish first
d: Expand the scope to the other sites before building anything
explanation: The loop is embed, find the problem worth solving, build fast with what exists, deploy into real workflows, drive adoption, expand. Waiting for new infrastructure delays value by months.

stem: A new tool produces good schedules in a sandbox, but planners must retype them into the ERP to use them. Which FDE loop step is unfinished?
a: Embedding with the client's operations team
b: Finding the problem worth solving
c: Deploying into the real workflow
d: Expanding to the next site or use case
explanation: Value appears only when the tool sits inside the work people already do. A sandbox that needs manual retyping is built, but not deployed into the real workflow.

stem: In the FDE loop, when should a deployment expand to new use cases?
a: As soon as the contract allows additional billable work
b: Once value is delivered and adopted in the first one
c: Before go-live, so the roadmap impresses the steering committee
d: When the vendor releases a new version of the product
explanation: Expansion is the last step of the loop and follows delivered, adopted value. Widening the scope before the first use case holds spreads the team thin and proves nothing.

stem: An integrator proposes one team to scope, another to build and a third to run the tool. What does the FDE model prefer?
a: Three specialized teams, each bound by a clear contract
b: A separate run team that takes over right at go-live
c: A consulting team to scope, then offshore developers to build
d: One person accountable from scoping to steady state
explanation: Each handoff loses context and dilutes accountability. In the FDE model the same person owns the outcome from scoping to steady state.

stem: Halfway through a project, the FDE who scoped it moves to a new client and a colleague takes over. What is mainly lost?
a: The context and accountability built since scoping
b: The software licences, which must be renegotiated
c: Finance's sign-off on the baseline, which must be redone
d: The discovery work, which must restart from month one
explanation: One person from scoping to steady state avoids handoff chains. A mid-project handover loses context nobody wrote down and blurs who owns the outcome.

stem: Your scheduling tool has just gone live at Ferralux. When does the FDE's accountability for the deployment end?
a: At go-live, once the client has signed the acceptance form
b: When the code has been delivered and fully documented
c: When the new routine has reached steady state
d: At the end of the first three months of the engagement
explanation: The same person owns the outcome from scoping to steady state. Go-live is where data and adoption problems show up, so handing over there leaves them without an owner.

stem: A sales director wants FDEs to carry a licence quota to speed up expansion. What does the FDE model say?
a: Agree, since FDEs know the client better than anyone
b: Refuse: expansion should follow delivered value
c: Agree, but only for renewals of existing licences
d: Refuse, because FDEs are too junior to negotiate deals
explanation: FDEs carry no sales quota. Their credibility on the floor rests on solving the client's problem, and expansion follows the value they deliver, not a target.

stem: The CEO wants the new tool on all eight sites at once to save time. What does the FDE way recommend?
a: Prove it on one site first, then extend to the others
b: Launch on all eight sites together, then fix issues site by site as they appear
c: Start with the two smallest sites to limit the risk
d: Run a three-month paper study of all eight sites first
explanation: Lighthouse first: one site proves the gains in the P&L and reveals the real issues before they are multiplied by eight. Extension then follows a proven model.

stem: At the lighthouse site, usage is strong but finance has not reconciled the gains. What should happen before extending?
a: Nothing more, since strong usage shows the tool delivers value
b: Survey the users to confirm they save time each week
c: Reconcile the gains to the P&L first
d: Rebuild the tool so each site gets its own version
explanation: The lighthouse proves value with gains reconciled to the P&L, not with usage or user surveys. Extending on usage alone multiplies an unproven case.

stem: The FDE proposes meeting the client team once a month to limit disruption. What does the course recommend?
a: Monthly is enough if the FDE sends good written reports
b: A weekly operating rhythm with the client team
c: Daily stand-ups with the plant director until go-live
d: Meetings only when a problem comes up, to save time on both sides
explanation: A weekly operating rhythm with the client team catches issues while they are small. A monthly cadence learns of problems weeks late, when they are harder to fix.

stem: The FDE works closely with the planners, but the plant director has not been involved since kickoff. What is missing?
a: Regular leadership reviews to steer and remove blockers
b: A larger FDE team present on the site every day
c: A detailed weekly written report sent to IT
d: A second kickoff meeting with all the plant staff
explanation: The operating rhythm has two layers: weekly work with the client team and regular leadership reviews. Without the second, decisions only leaders can take stall the project.

stem: A deployment has missed the stop criteria agreed at launch, and the team asks for three more months. What should leadership do?
a: Grant the extension, since stopping wastes the money already spent
b: Extend, but cut the scope down to the easiest part of the problem
c: Hand the project to a different vendor and keep going
d: Apply the agreed criteria: stop, and record what was learned
explanation: Explicit stop criteria let a failing initiative end on agreed facts rather than sunk cost. Some AI initiatives are expected to fail; that is part of approving them like capex.

stem: A plant manager asks the FDE to keep a failed trial run from the sponsor until a fix is ready. What should the FDE do?
a: Agree, since the plant manager is the daily contact on site
b: Agree, provided the fix is ready within two weeks
c: Mention it in the final project report at the end
d: Inform the sponsor now, with the cause and the plan
explanation: The no-surprises rule holds whoever asks for silence: bad news goes to the sponsor immediately, with its cause and a plan. A sponsor who finds out later stops trusting the project.

stem: A client needs a plant-specific purge rule that the product does not model. Where should the FDE build it?
a: In a fork of the product made for this client
b: In the deployment layer, as client-specific context
c: Nowhere: tell the client the product cannot do it
d: In the core product, released to every other client
explanation: Client-specific context belongs in the deployment layer, where it is maintained without touching the product. A fork per client becomes impossible to upgrade.

stem: The FDE finds the product cannot handle multi-plant inventory, which many clients need. What should the FDE do?
a: Fork the product and add the feature for this client
b: Rebuild the feature inside this client's deployment layer
c: Escalate it to the software partner as a product gap
d: Drop the use case, since the product does not cover it
explanation: A gap many clients share is a product gap: escalate it to the software partner. Rebuilding it in each deployment, or forking, leaves every client on its own version.

stem: Why does the FDE way avoid forking the product for each client?
a: Most enterprise licence contracts forbid modified copies
b: Clients do not want features specific to their plant
c: Forked code runs more slowly than the original product
d: Every fix and upgrade would have to be redone per client
explanation: A fork per client turns every fix and upgrade into a separate project. Client context goes in the deployment layer; shared gaps go back to the product.

stem: In a field interview with a planner, which question yields the most reliable information?
a: How should scheduling ideally work in this plant?
b: Can you walk me through how you built yesterday's schedule?
c: What do you think of the current ERP system?
d: Would an AI tool make your day-to-day job easier, in your own view?
explanation: Ask for a real, recent instance. Descriptions of how things should work reproduce the official process; the last real case reveals workarounds and hidden rules.

stem: A plant manager says 'scheduling is a mess.' What is the first step in framing this as a problem?
a: Collect the features planners want in the new scheduling software
b: Benchmark the scheduling tools available on the market
c: State it with a metric, a perimeter and a baseline
d: Agree a go-live date with the plant manager first
explanation: A complaint is not a problem statement. Framing turns it into something testable: which metric, on which perimeter, measured against which baseline.

stem: Which problem statement is framed well enough to test?
a: Planners lose far too much time on scheduling every week
b: Line 3 changeover hours, now 120 a month, fall 20% by June
c: Use AI to improve scheduling performance across the plant
d: Make scheduling smarter, faster and more reliable for everyone
explanation: It names a metric, a perimeter and a baseline, so success or failure can be measured. The others describe a wish, not a testable problem.
flags: reviewer note: key only concrete numbers

stem: Noor's problem statement reads: 'Cut scrap on the extrusion lines by 15%.' What is still missing to make it testable?
a: The baseline scrap rate it is measured against
b: The name of the AI model that will be used
c: A list of the plant's other quality problems
d: The vendor's estimate of the expected return on investment
explanation: A 15% cut means nothing without its starting point. Metric and perimeter are there; the baseline is what makes the claim testable.

stem: Sam frames 'cut late deliveries by 30%' for the whole group, but only one plant's data is accessible. What should change?
a: Keep the group perimeter and estimate the other plants
b: Replace the metric with a user satisfaction score
c: Raise the target to 50% to cover the uncertainty
d: Narrow the perimeter to the plant you can measure
explanation: The perimeter must be one where the metric and its baseline can actually be measured. A group-wide claim built on estimates cannot be tested.

stem: You are framing a scheduling problem. Which metric should anchor the statement?
a: Weekly logins to the new scheduling tool
b: Planner satisfaction score in a survey
c: Number of features delivered per sprint
d: Changeover hours on the lines in scope
explanation: The metric must measure the business outcome the complaint is about. Logins, satisfaction and features measure activity around the tool, not whether the problem shrank.

stem: To learn how changeovers really happen on line 2, whom should you interview first?
a: The plant manager, who sees every line on the site
b: The IT team that maintains the MES data
c: The supplier who sold the line's equipment
d: The operators who perform them on each shift
explanation: Operators know the real sequence, the workarounds and the exceptions. Managers describe the official process, and interviewing only them reproduces it.

stem: In an interview, a planner mentions 'my little file' she checks before releasing orders. What should you do?
a: Ask her to show it and walk through what it checks
b: Note it and move on to the official process
c: Tell her the new tool will soon replace the file
d: Ask IT to import the file into the data warehouse
explanation: Personal spreadsheets often hold the hidden rules the official systems lack. Seeing one used on a real case reveals what the model must encode.

stem: An operator says the line 'runs exactly as the procedure says, apart from Fridays.' What should you do?
a: Model the standard procedure and leave the exception out
b: Ask the manager whether the Friday exception is approved
c: Ask about last Friday and walk through what happened
d: Log it as a data quality issue for the IT team
explanation: Exceptions are where hidden rules live. Walking through the last real case turns a passing remark into a rule the model can encode.

stem: A manager describes a clean process; the operators' answers reveal several workarounds. Which account do you design from?
a: The manager's, because it is the approved process
b: An average of both, to keep everyone on side
c: The operators', checked against real recent cases
d: Neither: rely only on the data held in the MES
explanation: The design must fit how the work is actually done. Workarounds signal rules or constraints the official process misses; verify them on real cases.

stem: Which line belongs in a naive-deployment failure memo for a scheduling tool?
a: Some users may resist the change in the first weeks after go-live
b: AI carries a range of inherent risks that the project team will need to monitor and manage carefully
c: Night shift reverts to its spreadsheet within two weeks: rush orders are missing
d: The project team will do its very best to limit any disruption
explanation: The memo predicts concretely what breaks, who reacts and by when. Vague statements about resistance or risk give the steering committee nothing to act on.

stem: Alex has finished the naive-deployment failure memo. What should happen to it?
a: Keep it in the team folder to avoid alarming the client
b: Send it to the vendor's support team for their records
c: Take it to the steering committee to agree mitigations
d: Share it with the operators after the first incident
explanation: The memo exists so the steering committee can decide on mitigations in advance. Hiding it to avoid alarm defeats its purpose and breaks the no-surprises rule.

stem: When should the naive-deployment failure memo be written?
a: At kickoff, before discovery has started
b: Before go-live, early enough to act on it
c: After the first week of running in production
d: Once the client has reported a first problem
explanation: Its value is prediction: written before go-live, it lets the team fix what would break. At kickoff too little is known; after go-live it becomes a post-mortem.

stem: Alex's failure memo predicts that maintenance will ignore the tool's night-shift alerts. What should Alex do about it?
a: Wait and see whether the prediction comes true
b: Agree a mitigation and an owner with maintenance
c: Report the maintenance team's attitude to HR
d: Leave maintenance managers to deal with it later
explanation: A predicted failure is only useful if someone acts on it. Agreeing a mitigation and an owner with the people concerned turns the forecast into prevention.

stem: A sponsor calls the failure memo pessimistic and bad for morale. What is the best response?
a: Replace it with a list of the expected benefits
b: Soften it so that only technical risks remain in it
c: Share it with the IT team only, not the committee
d: Predicted failures can be fixed before they cost trust
explanation: The memo is not pessimism but prevention. Failures named in advance can be mitigated; the same failures discovered after go-live cost the project its credibility.

stem: Sam used an AI assistant to write a SQL query summing scrap by line. What should Sam do before the numbers go to the client?
a: Switch to the most capable AI assistant available
b: Ask the assistant to review and double-check its own query for errors
c: Reconcile totals with a source report the client already uses
d: Note in the report that AI produced the query
explanation: Use AI tools freely for speed, but trust comes from checking outputs against source data. Asking the same tool to check itself is not independent verification.

stem: Your team wants to ban AI coding tools on the project to avoid errors. What does the course recommend?
a: Ban them for anything that touches production data
b: Use them freely, and check outputs against source data
c: Allow them only for documentation and slide writing
d: Use them, and trust whatever passes the compiler and tests
explanation: AI tools speed up the work; the discipline lies in verification. A ban gives up the speed, while trusting unchecked output gives up the client's trust.

stem: An AI assistant summarized 200 maintenance logs into five root causes for the steering committee. What should the FDE do first?
a: Present it, since the summary reads clearly and fluently
b: Ask a second AI tool whether it agrees with the summary
c: Present it with a note that the figures are AI-estimated
d: Spot-check each cause against the underlying logs
explanation: Fluent output is not verified output. Checking each cause against the source logs is what lets the FDE stand behind the findings in front of the committee.

stem: Your team used AI to extract 5,000 order lines from PDFs into a table. How should you verify the result?
a: Rely on the confidence score that the tool reports for each extracted line
b: Run the same extraction a second time and compare outputs
c: Compare a sample, odd cases included, with the source PDFs
d: Ask the planner whether the totals look about right to her
explanation: Verification means checking against source data, including the unusual cases where extraction fails. A tool's own score or a rerun is not an independent check.

stem: Why does the FDE way insist on checking AI-assisted work against source data?
a: Client trust rests on numbers that hold when checked
b: AI tools are too unreliable to be used for real work
c: Contracts require every line of code to be reviewed twice
d: Regulators require a manual audit of every AI output
explanation: AI tools are welcome for speed; credibility comes from outputs that survive a check against source data. One wrong figure found by the client costs more than the time saved.

stem: At handover, the client names an IT ticket queue as the owner of the new tool. What is the problem?
a: Ticket queues are too slow for an AI tool's incidents
b: No trained person owns the routine and its decisions
c: IT should not have access to production planning data
d: The vendor, not the client, should own the tool
explanation: The handover bar includes a trained internal owner. A ticket queue can log incidents but cannot judge the plans, adjust the rules or keep the routine alive.

stem: After go-live, usage stays high only on days when the FDE is on site. What does this say about handover?
a: The bar is not met: the routine still depends on the FDE
b: Handover can proceed, since average usage is high
c: The tool needs more features before anyone hands over
d: The plant manager should make usage mandatory first
explanation: The handover bar requires the new routine to hold without the FDE. Usage that falls when the FDE leaves shows the routine has not yet taken root.

stem: Two months after handover, the MES data feed stops silently and plans degrade for a week. What was missing?
a: A longer training course for the planners
b: An alert that fires when incoming data stops
c: A newer AI model with a much larger context window
d: A clause in the contract about MES availability
explanation: Production discipline includes monitoring. Without it, a silent failure is found by its consequences, here a week of bad plans, instead of by an alert.

stem: The new owner at Ferralux sees a failed nightly job and does not know what to do. What should the handover have included?
a: A runbook: known failures and the steps to recover
b: The FDE's personal phone number for emergencies
c: A full copy of the source code and its history
d: Admin rights for every planner to rerun the jobs
explanation: A runbook lets the internal owner recover from known failures without the FDE. Source code and a phone number keep the client dependent on its builder.

stem: Before leaving, how can the FDE test that the new routine holds without them?
a: Ask the sponsor to confirm it in a signed letter
b: Check that the tool has been live for at least a month
c: Survey the users on whether they feel ready to continue
d: Step away for a period and check the metric holds
explanation: The bar is the routine holding without the FDE, so test exactly that. Sign-offs, elapsed time and confidence surveys do not show what happens when the FDE is gone.

stem: On day one at Polymex Industries, the FDE is eager to see the lines. What comes first?
a: The site safety induction and its rules
b: A tour of the lines with the plant manager
c: Installing the data connectors on the MES
d: Interviewing the operators on the night shift
explanation: Safety rules come first on any site. No discovery goal, however urgent, justifies going onto the floor before the induction.

stem: You need input from operators on all three shifts. How do you plan the interviews?
a: Gather all operators in one meeting at 10 a.m.
b: Interview the day shift and assume the others work the same
c: Visit each shift, at times that suit its line
d: Send a written survey and wait for the answers
explanation: Shifts often work differently, each with its own workarounds. Respecting shift patterns means going to each shift at a time that does not disrupt production.

stem: An operator is mid-changeover when you arrive for a scheduled interview. What should you do?
a: Start the questions anyway, since the slot was agreed
b: Wait or come back, observing if they allow it
c: Ask the supervisor to have someone else finish the changeover
d: Cancel the interview and use the MES data instead
explanation: Respect for operators' time means production comes first. Watching the changeover, with their agreement, is often worth more than the interview itself.

stem: A senior operator says the tool's suggested sequence will damage a die, though the data says otherwise. What do you do?
a: Trust the data, since it is more objective than opinion
b: Escalate to the supervisor and let them settle the question
c: Note it for the next release and keep the current sequence
d: Take it seriously and check the case with the operator
explanation: Operators' expertise often holds rules the data lacks. Checking the case with them respects that expertise and may reveal a missing constraint before a die is damaged.

stem: A line lead invites you past a guard rail to see a sensor up close and save time. What do you do?
a: Decline and follow the site's safety rules
b: Accept, since the line lead knows the area best
c: Accept, but only while the line runs at low speed
d: Accept once you have signed the visitor log
explanation: Safety rules come first, whoever offers the shortcut. An FDE who breaks them endangers people and loses the floor's respect at once.

stem: Your monthly report to the account lead lists hours on site, lines of code shipped and slides delivered. What should it report instead?
a: Requirements gathered, documents written and workshops run with the client team
b: Hours billed against budget, with a forecast of the hours left to the end
c: Time to first value, named weekly users and the gain signed by finance
d: Features shipped per sprint and open bugs, sorted by their severity
explanation: An FDE is measured on what reaches the client's P&L: time to a decision taken with the system, weekly adoption by named users, and a gain finance signs. Hours, code and slides appear nowhere in the P&L.

stem: To understand why one line drifts at weekends, Sam proposes a chart of output per operator for the weekend crew. What do you do instead?
a: Analyse by machine and shift, with no operator names on any chart
b: Run the chart, but only share it with the site director and HR
c: Run the chart for one month, then delete it once the cause is found
d: Ask the weekend crew to vote on whether the chart may be produced
explanation: An FDE never collects data in a way that reads as monitoring people. Data watches machines, not operators; in France the works council is consulted before any tool that could monitor employees.

stem: The sponsor is sure the night shift causes the scrap increase. Your first data points elsewhere. How should your hypothesis tree treat his theory?
a: Leave it out, since the first data already points to another cause
b: Make it the root of the tree, since he is the one funding the work
c: Park it in an appendix, to be discussed once the results are in
d: Include it as one branch, with a prior and a test like the others
explanation: Neither accept nor dismiss the sponsor's culprit: write it in as one testable branch. If the data clears it, that test is what lets you move him without humiliating him.

stem: A plant manager says 'maintenance takes forever' and asks you to compare CMMS vendors. What do you do before looking at any vendor?
a: Collect the technicians' wish list of features for the new tool
b: Name the observable symptom and the gap as a number with its source
c: Estimate the budget the plant can spend on a new system this year
d: Benchmark the plant's maintenance costs against all of its sister sites
explanation: Climb the rungs: complaint, observable symptom, quantified gap, candidate causes. Deployments that jump from the complaint to a tool often find the real cause elsewhere, such as technicians waiting for parts.

stem: A site director asks for an OTIF analysis by month end. You learn that a corporate review of his site is in three weeks. Why does this matter for framing?
a: It only changes the deadline, not the problem you are framing
b: It means the hypothesis tree can be skipped to save some time
c: It shapes what solved means to him and what he must show upward
d: It is a political detail the analysis should keep well away from
explanation: Ask the question behind the question: who hurts, why now, what solved looks like to the sponsor. The same words mean a different problem three weeks before a corporate review.

stem: You want to learn how far a planner trusts the ERP's changeover times. Which question is most likely to give you a useful answer?
a: Don't you think the ERP's changeover times are often unreliable?
b: Is the changeover data in the ERP right, in your own opinion?
c: Why did you stop trusting the changeover times in the ERP?
d: If those times were wrong, where would you look first to check?
explanation: Open questions about a concrete case surface the real rules. A yes-or-no question gets a yes, a leading one returns your own idea, and 'why did you' sounds like an audit.

stem: The procedure says the plan is frozen each week; the planner says she rewrites it every day. How do you establish what really happens?
a: Count the plan changes in the change log and compare with interviews
b: Follow the procedure, since quality approved it and it is the reference
c: Follow the planner, since she is the one running the plan every day
d: Ask the site director to decide which of the two accounts is correct
explanation: The procedure is a hypothesis; the change log is the evidence. Map the true process from interviews and compute its loops from data, rather than trusting either account alone.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture

stem: You need to find who really holds the scheduling rules at a new site. Which question to operators and shift leaders finds them fastest?
a: Who is in charge of scheduling according to the org chart?
b: Who do you call when something goes wrong during the night?
c: Which department owns the written scheduling procedure here?
d: Who signed off the latest version of the planning process?
explanation: The informal network is the real map: the same two or three names come back when you ask who people call when the system fails. The expert the floor trusts is often missing from the org chart.

stem: You have two minutes with a site director to explain why on-time delivery fell. How do you open?
a: With the data sources and the method, so that he trusts the findings
b: With the history of the problem since January, in date order
c: With the answer and its size, then the decision you need from him
d: With the three hypotheses you tested, then your final conclusion
explanation: Executives triage in seconds: put the governing thought first, the answer and its so-what, then ask for one decision. Method and history belong underneath, for when he asks why.

stem: The controller's baseline will make next week's steering committee see a smaller gain than the sponsor expects. What should happen before the meeting?
a: Send the new numbers to all committee members by email the evening before
b: Present it in the meeting itself, so that everyone hears it at once
c: Keep the baseline off the agenda until finance has fully closed it
d: Meet the sponsor and the controller one to one, and adjust with them
explanation: Pre-wire: nobody should hear anything important for the first time in a meeting. Show each key person what concerns them in private, so the meeting becomes a formality.

stem: In a hallway chat, the controller agreed the formula for the baseline. The decision lives only in your notebook. What does the course expect?
a: A recap the same day, filed in the bundle as a decision with its source
b: Nothing more, since the controller keeps the official spreadsheet
c: A line in the next monthly steering pack, so that it is on record
d: A message in the team chat so that the other FDEs are aware of it
explanation: If it is not in the bundle, it did not happen. Decisions are concepts: who decided, when, on what evidence, written the same day so that four people tell the CFO the same number.

stem: Your v1 is used daily by the named planners, but an FDE still restarts a job by hand most mornings. Which exit criterion is still open?
a: Build: named users rely on v1 on the floor every single day
b: Find: the charter is signed by the sponsor before the build
c: Deploy: it runs two weeks without the FDE touching it
d: Expand: the next charter is signed for a new problem or site
explanation: Daily use by named users is the build exit, and it is met. Deployed means monitored, documented, owned by a named person in IT, and running two weeks without the FDE touching it.

stem: In week 3, the sales director asks you to add a quoting tool to the scheduling project, for the same planners. What do you do?
a: Add it quietly, since it helps the same users and costs little time
b: Refuse it outright, since it is not on the signed scope-in list
c: Start it in parallel, and report it to the sponsor once the scheduler has shipped
d: Take it to the steering committee and the decision log as a scope change
explanation: Every scope change goes through the steering committee and the decision log. Perimeter creep is how gains get laughed out of the room at month six; a flat refusal ignores a possibly valid request.

stem: At your kickoff, the executive committee asks what would make you stop at week 4. Which answer meets the standard the course sets?
a: If the sponsor loses confidence in the approach at any point, we stop the work
b: If changeovers explain under a third of the OTIF loss by week 4, we stop
c: If progress at week 4 is slower than planned, we review the plan
d: If the team judges the model is not good enough by week 4, we stop
explanation: A kill criterion is measurable, tied to a gate, and agreed in the kickoff before anyone is attached to the solution. Confidence, slow progress or the team's judgment can be argued forever.

stem: The build starts Monday. A sponsor, an IT owner, a product owner and users are named, but no controller. What should you do?
a: Name the controller before the build, as owner of the baseline and gain
b: Start the build and bring finance in once a first gain becomes visible
c: Let the FDE team compute the baseline until finance has time for it
d: Ask the sponsor to sign off the gain himself at the end of the project
explanation: Five client roles need a name before the build, and the controller owns the baseline, the formula and the gain. A baseline built later, or by the FDE, is a fight with finance at month six.
flags: test-wise: answerable from cues (longest, repeats stem words)

stem: In shadow mode, the system's plans now match the planner's on most days. What is the next step of the deployment?
a: She publishes the system's plan by default unless she objects
b: She starts from the system's plan, and every change needs a reason
c: Small repairs of a known class publish alone, with her informed
d: The system publishes the whole plan, and she reviews only the exceptions
explanation: Deployment runs shadow, co-pilot, default, then autonomous by class. After shadow comes co-pilot, where each change carries a reason the improvement loop can use. The whole plan never publishes alone.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop

stem: The planner moves an order off the line the system chose. Her reason: 'The customer would send it back.' What do you do next?
a: Write a rule keeping this customer's orders off that line from now on
b: Log it as a one-off preference and keep the system's original plan
c: Ask her whether it is because of a quality audit on that line
d: Keep asking why until the answer is a plant fact with an owner
explanation: The first answer is a consequence, not a rule. Ask why without suggesting the answer until you reach a fact that will hold next week, such as a line qualification, and the person who owns it.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop

stem: Your planning system keeps missing order changes that the scheduling clerk writes in a paper notebook. What does the course suggest?
a: Ask IT to add a field for these changes in the ERP's next scheduled upgrade
b: Have the model read photos of her notebook pages every evening
c: A small intake app where she records each change, structured and timed
d: Take these changes out of scope, since no system holds them today
explanation: Build mini-apps that collect what no system holds: event intake, overrides with a reason, execution capture. The data then arrives structured, timed and owned, instead of waiting for an ERP project.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop

stem: Your platform provides the solvers, the rules engine, permissions, audit and a model gateway. Which work on site belongs to your team?
a: A faster solver tuned to the specific lines and products of this plant
b: The plant's rules, the field mappings and who may do what
c: A new audit log and secret store built for this client's security team
d: A dedicated model gateway with this client's own prompt templates
explanation: Compose the platform; your code is the architecture and the plant. A local solver or harness becomes another orphan for IT, while the rules, mappings and permissions are what only the site can give.
source: Day 3, the platform and the first loop

stem: Day 2 of the project: group IT says any new cloud service needs a six-week security review. Your plan assumed access in week one. What do you do?
a: Start the review today and work on exports while it runs
b: Ask the sponsor to waive the review for this one project
c: Pause the project until the security review is complete
d: Use a personal cloud account until the approval arrives
explanation: Technical dead ends have known moves; the mistake is improvising around the rules. Start the review on day one and keep working on exports, so the six weeks are not lost.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: Your Verifier finds that the gain you showed the CFO two weeks ago is overstated by a third. Steering is on Friday. What do you do?
a: Correct it in the Friday steering pack, with a short footnote
b: Tell the sponsor and controller within a day, with the corrected figure
c: Explain it on Friday, when there is enough time to give the full context
d: Keep the figure and lower next quarter's target to compensate
explanation: Announce a data error first, before anyone finds it, with the corrected figure and what it changes, then add the check that would have caught it. Trust lost by a correction returns; a cover-up does not.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: The sponsor has skipped two weekly reviews, and only he can unblock group security. You asked him in private, with a date. Nothing moved. What next?
a: Go around him and contact group security directly yourself
b: Wait until his workload eases after the coming board review
c: Escalate to whoever sold the project, so scope or sponsor changes
d: Raise his absence in front of everyone at the next steering committee
explanation: A sponsor who does not act is a contract problem, not a mood: name the act, ask in private with a date, then take it back to whoever sold the project. Exposing him in public loses him for good.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: Go-live is next week. Site IT has nobody to own the app yet, and the planner offers to 'keep an eye on it'. What do you do?
a: Go live, and stay on site yourself until an owner is found
b: Go live, with the planner as owner until IT finds someone
c: Go live, and hand the app to the vendor's support desk
d: Hold go-live until the client names an owner in IT
explanation: A named owner at the client before go-live, or no go-live. Deployed means monitored, documented and owned by a named person in IT; anything else leaves an orphan application.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: Your scheduler works at the first plant. The COO wants it at a second plant that runs at 64% capacity. What do you do first?
a: Copy the first plant's rules and thresholds to save the local team time
b: Redo the true-process walk there, since its problem may not be planning
c: Deploy the same release now and tune it there after go-live
d: Have the first plant's planner train the second plant's planner
explanation: What worked on one site is a hypothesis on the next. A plant at 64% capacity may lack orders, not a better plan; start again from its true process and ask what it does better.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: You take a working planning system to a second plant. Which part do you rebuild there with its local owners rather than reuse?
a: The local rules, data connectors and thresholds
b: The ontology core and the rules engine behind it
c: The platform's permissions, harness and audit trail
d: The solvers and the structure of the scorecard
explanation: Reuse the core, rebuild the edge: the ontology core, platform, solvers and scorecard travel. Local rules, connectors, thresholds, the first user and the rituals are rebuilt with the people who own them.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales

stem: Your coding agent says 'all tests pass' after fixing an OEE calculation. In the diff, you see it changed the test's expected value. What do you do?
a: Accept it, since the tests pass and the build is now green
b: Delete the test, since it was clearly wrong in the first place
c: Ask the agent to confirm in writing that the new value is right
d: Restore the test and have it change the code, not the test
explanation: Use AI tools for speed, and earn trust by checking. A test changed to pass checks nothing; recompute the value from the raw rows if in doubt, and record the rule in CLAUDE.md.
source: Doctrine, deployment and the FDE way

stem: Your app shows plant OEE at 71%. Your Verifier, computing it independently, gets 64%. The demo is in ten minutes. What do you do?
a: Find the cause of the gap before showing either of the two numbers
b: Show the app's number, since the code behind it has been fully tested
c: Show the average of the two figures, and mention the uncertainty
d: Show both figures and let the client decide which one to trust
explanation: Every number you show must survive someone else's check. Demo only when both pairs agree or you can explain the difference; a gap often hides an average of ratios or a unit error.

stem: You are writing a project kickoff document for a client's executive committee. What belongs on its first page?
a: The team's credentials and its references in the client's sector
b: A description of the six phases of the method you will follow
c: The problem, the gain with its condition, and the decision asked
d: The full table of assumptions behind the low, base and high cases
explanation: Answer first: page one carries the governing thought, the size with its condition, and the decision you ask for. Assumptions and method support it further down.

stem: Reading the signed proposal against its data annex, you find pre-sales promised a gain measured on data the plant does not record. When do you raise it?
a: At the kickoff: what you correct, why, and what you propose instead
b: At week 6, once the project has collected enough data to prove the point
c: During the build, by quietly narrowing the scope of the work
d: Only with your account lead, so that the client does not worry
explanation: Pre-sales promised something; the kickoff is where you correct it, never week 6. A promise corrected on day one costs a hard meeting; discovered at week 6, it costs the project.

stem: In your first two weeks at a new plant, how should you take part in the daily production meeting?
a: Present your first findings each morning to show early progress
b: Attend weekly only, since the daily meeting is operational detail
c: Send a junior to take notes, so that you can spend the time building
d: Attend every day, note which numbers are contested, speak when asked
explanation: The morning meeting is where the plant thinks out loud and names problems before they reach any system. Being there daily and listening earns credibility; early findings can wait.

stem: An expert planner resists the new scheduling tool. What usually works best?
a: Escalate to the plant director so that tool usage is enforced from above
b: Move the planner off the project to avoid friction
c: Make the planner a co-author: encode their rules, show their data
d: Tie tool usage targets to the planner's bonus from day one
explanation: Resistance usually signals a fear, such as losing expertise or status. Turning the expert from suspect into co-author puts their rules in the model and their name on the result.

stem: Why reshuffle teams around a new AI asset, even when headcount is a small part of the gain?
a: An asset dropped into an unchanged organization gets absorbed by it
b: Payroll reduction is where most of the program's value really comes from
c: Employee representatives require a new organization chart
d: New roles make the program more visible to the board
explanation: The reshuffle is not the gain; it is what makes the other gain lines reachable. Unchanged teams keep taking yesterday's decisions with today's tool.

stem: What does the history of factory electrification teach about AI adoption?
a: Early adopters capture most of the value
b: Gains came once work was redesigned and a new generation trained
c: Adoption only takes off once the cost of the technology has collapsed
d: Regulation is the main driver of adoption
explanation: Electric motors paid off decades after they arrived, once factories were redesigned around them (Paul David). Plan the redesign, and overweight training for the incoming generation.

stem: Two weeks after go-live at Polymex Industries, schedule adherence is below its old level. The plant manager wants to roll back. What do you advise?
a: Roll back now and relaunch the tool once the whole team has been retrained
b: Hold course: a dip before the rise was expected and planned for
c: Enforce the tool through daily usage KPIs so adherence recovers fast
d: Accept that the planners' old method was better and keep it
explanation: Performance dips before it rises on the change curve; the plan should have budgeted for it. Rolling back at the dip throws away the change just before it pays.

stem: Go-live is planned for March. What should the plan include for the performance dip expected in the first weeks?
a: Targets raised early, to push the team through the dip faster
b: A rollback to the old method at the first drop in output
c: Buffers in targets and capacity, plus extra support on the floor
d: A message to the floor that results will improve from the first day
explanation: On the change curve, performance dips before it rises. Planning buffers and support for the dip keeps it from being read as failure and triggering a rollback.

stem: Planners have stopped arguing against the new tool and now try it on a few orders, asking many questions. Which stage of the change curve is this?
a: Denial
b: Resistance
c: Exploration
d: Commitment
explanation: The curve runs denial, resistance, exploration, commitment. Trying the tool and asking questions is exploration; support matters most here.

stem: A quality lead raises a new technical objection each time the previous one is answered. What is the most likely reading?
a: The tool has deep technical flaws that the project team has missed
b: The quality lead is being irrational and is best kept away from the project
c: The objections call for a longer written answer from the vendor
d: A fear, such as losing status or being blamed, drives the objections
explanation: Resistance usually signals a fear: status, expertise, job or blame. When answers do not end objections, the argument is not the real issue; address the fear.

stem: Senior planners fear the tool will be used to blame them for late orders. Which response addresses this best?
a: Agree openly how plan errors will be reviewed, as a team and without blame
b: Show benchmark data proving that the tool's plans beat the plans they make by hand today
c: Promise them that tool usage will not be monitored in any way
d: Escalate to the sponsor so the concern does not slow the project
explanation: Address the fear, not only the argument. Accuracy data answers the argument but leaves the fear of blame intact.

stem: During co-authoring, an expert planner's sequencing rule contradicts the ERP data. What should the team do?
a: Keep the ERP version, since it is the official system of record
b: Encode the rule as stated, without checking, to keep the expert on side
c: Test the rule with the expert on real cases, then encode it if it holds
d: Drop the rule to keep the model simple until after go-live
explanation: Co-authorship means the expert's rules go into the model, checked against real cases. Ignoring them loses the rule and the expert; encoding them blindly loses accuracy.

stem: The tool will soon publish plans built on rules from the plant's best planner. Why put that planner's name on the result?
a: It makes the planner formally accountable, in writing, for each plan the tool issues from now on
b: It gives the planner ownership, so they defend the tool instead of attacking it
c: It lets management compare the planner's output with colleagues' output
d: It shows the vendor which users should be trained first
explanation: Experts become co-authors: their rules in the model, their name on the result. The suspect becomes the author, with a stake in the tool's success.

stem: The project team leaves in three months. Who should carry the tool afterward?
a: The IT helpdesk, which already supports every other application running in the plant today
b: The vendor's customer success manager, through quarterly calls
c: Whichever planner happens to use the tool the most, informally
d: An internal operational champion with a formal role and legitimacy
explanation: An internal operational champion with a formal role, legitimacy and a direct line to the software teams carries the tools after the project team leaves.

stem: Noor volunteers to be the tool's champion, on top of her full planning job, with no title or time set aside. What is missing?
a: Nothing: volunteering shows the motivation a champion needs most
b: A deeper technical background so she can change the code herself
c: A formal role and the legitimacy to speak for the floor
d: A bonus tied to the number of tool logins on her team
explanation: Goodwill is not enough. The champion needs a formal role and legitimacy, plus a direct line to the software teams, to keep the tool alive after the project ends.

stem: Why should the tool's champion usually come from operations rather than from IT?
a: Peers on the floor trust someone who knows their work and its constraints
b: IT staff are not allowed to change production schedules or planning data in most plants
c: Operations staff need much less training on the software itself
d: IT will be busy with integration work for years after go-live
explanation: The champion is operational: legitimacy with the people who use the tool daily is what carries it. IT remains a partner, reached through the champion's direct line.

stem: A champion's direct line to the software team matters mainly because:
a: It lets the champion bypass the plant's IT security rules
b: Floor needs reach the people who can change the tool, quickly
c: It replaces the need for a steering committee after go-live
d: The software team can then monitor each user's activity in detail
explanation: Without a direct line, requests from the floor stall and the tool falls behind the work. The champion turns floor needs into changes.

stem: The new tool now does sequencing that took two planners all day. Which reshuffle fits the course?
a: Keep both planners in their old roles to avoid disruption on the floor
b: Remove both planner positions at once to book the payroll saving
c: Let each planner decide individually how to use the time that was freed
d: Redesign their roles around exceptions and capacity decisions the tool surfaces
explanation: An asset dropped into an unchanged organization gets absorbed by it. Redesigning roles around the new work is what makes the other gain lines reachable.

stem: The CEO wants to announce the AI program at next week's all-hands, before the first tool works. What do you advise?
a: Build quietly until it demonstrably works, then reveal it
b: Announce it now so that every employee has plenty of time to prepare for it
c: Announce now, and promise that no role will ever change
d: Announce only the budget and keep the scope confidential
explanation: Build in silence until the asset demonstrably works. An early announcement invites fears and rumors with nothing yet to show.

stem: The tool is ready to be shown to the whole plant. Besides the tool itself, what should the presentation include?
a: A live demo, with the rest of the details to follow in later months
b: The vendor's roadmap of upcoming features and releases
c: The usage targets each planner must hit from the first week
d: The capture plan, the new team organization and the training
explanation: The reveal comes as a package: the working asset, the capture plan, the new team and the training. A demo alone leaves people guessing what changes for them.

stem: The training budget for a new planning tool is limited. Where does the course suggest putting extra weight?
a: On the most senior staff, who have the most habits to unlearn
b: On managers, who can then cascade the training to their teams
c: On one go-live session that covers everyone at the same time
d: On the incoming generation who will run the redesigned work
explanation: Electrification paid off once work was redesigned and a new generation trained. Overweight training for the people who will carry the new way of working for decades.

stem: A project plan treats change management as a two-day training at go-live. What is wrong with it?
a: Two days is too short; it should be a full week of classroom training
b: Change runs through the whole project, starting at scoping
c: Nothing, provided the training covers every feature of the tool
d: Training should be left to the vendor to save time for the project team
explanation: Change management is not training at the end. It runs through the project: experts as co-authors, a champion, a reshuffled team, a planned reveal.

stem: A year after go-live, planners are back on spreadsheets; the tool still runs on its original rules. What was most likely missing?
a: A strict mandate that blocks the use of spreadsheets for planning on the plant network
b: A second round of go-live training for every planner
c: A regular feedback loop where the client says how its needs changed
d: An upgrade to the latest model release from the vendor
explanation: Needs change after go-live. Without regular moments where the client says what changed, tools decay on autopilot and people drift back to their own workarounds.

stem: Camille, an expert scheduler, fears that once her rules are in the tool she will no longer be needed. What addresses this best?
a: Being clear early about her role after go-live, built on her expertise
b: Showing her that the tool's plans are already more accurate than her own
c: Postponing the question until after go-live to avoid tension now
d: Telling her that questions about jobs are outside the project's scope
explanation: Resistance usually signals a fear, here for her job. Address the fear itself; proving the tool better than her answers the argument and sharpens the fear.

stem: While a tool is built in silence, who outside the core project team should know about it?
a: The sponsor and the experts who co-author the model
b: Nobody at all, the expert planners included, until the reveal
c: The whole plant, through a regular project newsletter
d: Only the vendor, since it supplies the software
explanation: Building in silence means no public announcement before the asset works, not secrecy from the sponsor or from the experts whose rules go into the model.

stem: How should you describe the scheduling tool's goal to the shop floor?
a: In headcount terms: how many planning hours the plant can now cut
b: In throughput terms: more good output from the same lines
c: In technical terms: the model and data platform behind it
d: In cost terms: the euro savings finance expects each year
explanation: Communicate in throughput terms. Headcount framing feeds the job fear behind resistance; technical framing means little to the people affected.

stem: Employee representatives must be consulted on new work tools at your site. When should you involve them?
a: Early, as required, before the rollout is already decided
b: After go-live, once the results of the tool can speak for themselves
c: Only if staff raise a formal complaint about the tool
d: At the public reveal, at the same time as everyone else
explanation: Where consultation is required, involve representatives early. Bringing them in after decisions are made turns a formal step into a conflict.

stem: IT has blocked the tool's network access for three weeks and the team cannot resolve it. Whose job is it to remove the blocker?
a: The steering committee's, at its next scheduled meeting
b: The champion's, through informal contacts within IT
c: The sponsor's, who has the authority to clear it now
d: The vendor account manager's, through their IT contacts
explanation: The sponsor removes blockers; the steering committee keeps the cadence. Waiting for the next committee lets a three-week block become a two-month one.

stem: In a deployment, what is the main job of the steering committee?
a: Remove day-to-day blockers as soon as they come up on site, without waiting
b: Approve each change to the tool's code before it ships
c: Stand in for the sponsor whenever the sponsor is unavailable
d: Keep the cadence: regular reviews of progress, issues and decisions
explanation: The steering committee keeps the cadence; the sponsor removes blockers. A committee that waits to clear daily blockers is too slow for them.

stem: Which signal best shows that a planning team has reached commitment on the change curve?
a: Logins have risen every week since go-live, on all shifts and all lines
b: Planners propose improvements and defend the tool to peers
c: Complaints about the tool have stopped since it went live
d: Every planner has completed the full training course
explanation: Commitment shows in ownership: people improve the tool and stand up for it. Silence, logins and training records can coexist with quiet resistance.

stem: Operators override the scheduler's plan 30% of the time. What should the FDE do first?
a: Lock the plan in the system so that operators can no longer change it at all
b: Send the operators back through the training program
c: Report low adoption of the tool to the project sponsor
d: Study the reasons: each override points to a missing rule or bad data
explanation: Overrides are information. Each reveals a constraint the model lacks or data that is wrong; fixing them is how trust and accuracy rise together.

stem: The override log shows planners always move one order type off line 2 on night shift. What does this most likely reveal?
a: Night-shift planners need refresher training on how to use the tool's plans
b: A missing constraint, such as a night-shift skill or tooling limit
c: The tool is right and the night shift is ignoring its plans
d: Random noise that will average out over the coming months
explanation: A systematic override points to a rule the model lacks or data that is wrong. Treating it as a training or discipline issue throws that information away.

stem: When a user overrides a plan, what should the tool capture so the team can learn from it?
a: Only the count, so the override rate can be tracked over time
b: The user's name, so that repeat overriders can be retrained
c: Nothing, since logging overrides tends to discourage users
d: The changed decision plus a short, structured reason for it
explanation: Overrides are information only if their reasons are captured. A count shows the size of the problem, not which rule or data is missing.

stem: The override rate fell from 30% to 5% in two months. What should the FDE check before celebrating?
a: That logins on the tool rose by the same proportion
b: That the sponsor has been told the tool is now trusted
c: That the drop came from fixed rules and data, not from users giving up
d: That the remaining overrides are spread evenly across all users and all shifts
explanation: Fewer overrides is good news only if missing rules and bad data were fixed. Users who stop overriding but decide elsewhere have abandoned the tool, not adopted it.

stem: The vendor dashboard shows 95% daily logins. What better shows real adoption?
a: The average length of each user's session per day
b: The number of reports exported from the tool each week
c: The share of staff who completed the full training course on the tool
d: The share of decisions actually taken with the tool's plans
explanation: Adoption is not usage. Count decisions taken with the tool and the reasons for overrides; logins and sessions measure presence, not decisions.
flags: reviewer note: overlap logins (with CHG-3-006, CHG-3-007)

stem: Planners log in every morning, then build the actual plan in their own spreadsheet. How should the FDE read this?
a: Usage without adoption: find why decisions still happen outside the tool
b: Successful adoption, since every planner logs in to the tool daily
c: A training gap, best fixed with extra classroom sessions for every planner on site
d: A discipline problem, best fixed by blocking the spreadsheets
explanation: Logging in is not deciding. The spreadsheet holds rules or data the tool lacks, or a fear not yet addressed; finding which is the work.
flags: reviewer note: overlap logins (with CHG-3-005, CHG-3-007)

stem: Management wants to tie bonuses to tool login counts from day one. What is the likely effect?
a: Adoption rises, since the bonus gives every user a clear target
b: Resistance disappears once money is at stake for each user
c: Logins rise while real decisions keep being made elsewhere
d: Data quality improves because users enter more information
explanation: Mandating usage through KPIs from day one buys logins, not decisions. It also hides the override reasons that would improve the tool.
flags: reviewer note: overlap logins (with CHG-3-005, CHG-3-006)

stem: Alex, a respected shift leader, calls the new tool 'a toy'. Which first move does the course favor?
a: Ask his manager to add tool usage to his yearly objectives
b: Show him the vendor's case studies from other plants
c: Leave him out until the rest of the team is convinced
d: Use the tool to solve one of his daily pains first
explanation: To turn a skeptic, solve one of their pains first, show their own data and give them authorship. Mandates and outside case studies do not address why he doubts.

stem: A skeptical quality lead doubts the tool's defect predictions. Which evidence is most likely to persuade her?
a: Accuracy figures from the vendor's benchmark at other plants
b: The predictions replayed on her own line's past batches
c: A demo on a clean sample dataset prepared by the team
d: Testimonials from users at a sister site of the group
explanation: Skeptics trust their own data. A replay on her line's history answers her doubt in her terms; benchmarks and clean demos invite the reply 'not here'.

stem: Sam, the most skeptical planner, keeps finding errors in the tool's plans. How can the FDE best use this?
a: Make him the reviewer who writes the missing rules, credited by name
b: Limit his access to the tool so that his criticism does not spread
c: Collect his errors into a formal report for the software vendor
d: Ask him to hold his findings until the next scheduled release
explanation: Give the skeptic authorship. His error-finding is the best source of missing rules, and authorship turns the critic into a defender.

stem: A maintenance lead objects that the tool ignores planned stops. You reply at once with accuracy statistics. What did you skip?
a: Confirming the objection with his manager before you replied
b: Sending the objection to the vendor for a formal answer
c: Acknowledging his concern and clarifying the case behind it
d: Waiting for the steering committee to rule on the objection
explanation: Objection handling runs acknowledge, clarify, answer with evidence, confirm. Statistics fired back unasked miss the specific case and make the person feel unheard.

stem: A planner says the plans ignore a cleaning step on line 3. What is the strongest answer?
a: Overall accuracy figures showing that the tool performs well across all lines on average
b: Real plans showing whether the step is handled, or a fix if it is not
c: A promise that the vendor will look at it in a later release
d: An explanation that the cleaning step is a minor edge case
explanation: Answer with evidence on the specific case. If the objection is right, it is an override-style signal: fix the rule and show the fix.

stem: You have answered a planner's objection about rush orders. What closes the loop?
a: Logging the objection as resolved in the project tracker
b: Reporting the outcome to her manager the same day
c: Moving on quickly so the meeting stays on schedule
d: Confirming with her that the answer resolves the concern
explanation: The last step is confirm: check with the person that the concern is resolved. Closing it on your own side leaves the objection alive on hers.

stem: You must tell a production manager that his team's data entry causes most plan errors. How should you open?
a: With the facts: the error log and the cases traced to data entry
b: With your view that his team needs more discipline in data entry
c: With praise, keeping the problem for the end of the meeting
d: With a reminder that the sponsor expects results this quarter
explanation: Difficult conversations start with facts before opinions. The traced cases give him something to examine instead of a judgment to defend against.

stem: In a tense review, a planner says the project 'is making him look incompetent'. Which reply follows the course?
a: Reassure him that the tool is right, so he has nothing at all to fear from it
b: Agree that some planners will struggle with the change
c: Separate him from the problem: the issue is the process, not his skill
d: End the meeting and report the conflict to the sponsor
explanation: Separate the person from the problem. Locating the issue in the process protects his standing and keeps the discussion on what to fix.

stem: How should a difficult conversation with a resistant department head end?
a: On a summary of everything that has gone wrong so far
b: On an agreed next step, with an owner and a date
c: On a reminder of what the sponsor expects from the department
d: Without commitments, to let emotions settle for a while
explanation: End on a next step. Without an owner and a date, the conversation changes nothing on the ground.

stem: A planner ignored a delay the tool had flagged, and a delivery was late. How should you raise it with him?
a: Start from the dated facts and look together at why the flag was missed
b: Remind him that the tool was right and that he must follow its plans
c: Raise it with his manager first so that it is handled formally
d: Let it pass, to protect the relationship with the planning team
explanation: Facts before opinions, and the person separated from the problem: looking at why the flag was missed may reveal a missing rule rather than a careless planner.

stem: How should operators be trained on a new dispatching tool?
a: In a single classroom day for all shifts, a week before go-live
b: Through e-learning videos to be completed before go-live
c: By the vendor, in a demo environment with sample data
d: At their workstation, on real cases, shift by shift
explanation: Train at the workstation, on real cases, shift by shift. Classroom and demo training teach features; the workstation teaches the job with the tool.

stem: Night shift gets little support after go-live and its plans drift. What helps most?
a: A recording of the day-shift training session for night staff
b: A phone hotline to the vendor's central support desk
c: Super-users on the night shift who coach colleagues on real cases
d: An email to night staff with the full user manual attached
